Let $\bm{A}_{n}$ and $\bm{B}_{n}$ be (possibly non-symmetric and random) matrix sequences of growing dimension. We write $\bm{A}_{n}\asymp\bm{B}_{n}$ if for every deterministic sequence of test matrices $\bm{\Theta}_{n}$ with uniformly bounded trace norm $\|\bm{{\bm{\Theta}}}_{n}\|_{\ast}:={\sf tr}(\sqrt{{\bm{\Theta}}^{\top}{\bm{\Theta}}})$ ,

$$ {\sf tr}\big(\bm{\Theta}_{n}(\bm{A}_{n}-\bm{B}_{n})\big)\longrightarrow 0\qquad\text{(almost surely, as }n\to\infty\text{)}. $$

Under Assumption 2.1, we can use Theorem 1 in [81], to infer that

$$ \big(\widehat{{\bm{\Sigma}}}-zI\big)^{-1}\asymp\big(a_{n}{\bm{\Sigma}}-z\mathbf{I}_{p}\big)^{-1},\qquad\text{for }z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}_{+}, $$

where $a_{n}:=a_{n}(z)$ is the unique solution of the fixed-point equation:

$$ \frac{n}{p}\left(\frac{1}{a_{n}}-1\right)=\frac{1}{p}\,{\sf tr}\left[{\bm{\Sigma}}\big(a_{n}{\bm{\Sigma}}-z\mathbf{I}_{p}\big)^{-1}\right]. $$

The following Lemma characterizes the limit of $a_{n}$ when ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ is an $s$ -spiked model. This will be very useful when analyzing deterministic equivalents.

#### Lemma A.4.

Consider ${\bm{\Sigma}}=\sigma_{0}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{p}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}$ to be an $s$ -spiked covariance. For all $z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}_{+}$ let $a_{n}(z)$ be the unique solution of equation A.5. Then, there is a finite limit $a(z):=\lim_{n}a_{n}(z)$ and $a(z)$ satisfies

$$ a(z)=\frac{z}{\sigma_{0}^{2}}+\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,m(z)}=-z\underline{m}(z). $$

Finally, the following property will be useful in the computation of the deterministic equivalent of the spiked covariance matrix:

#### Proposition A.5.

Let ${\bm{\Sigma}}=\sigma_{0}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{p}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}$ be an $s$ -spiked covariance.

$$ (a_{n}{\bm{\Sigma}}-z\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}=\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z}\left[\mathbf{I}_{p}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{j}\,a_{n}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z+\delta_{j}\,a_{n}}\,\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\right]. $$

#### A.3.1 Proof of Lemma A.4

#### Proof.

In the following, we write $x_{n}\approx y_{n}$ if $x_{n}-y_{n}\to 0$ almost surely. Using the deterministic equivalent relation A.4 for $\bm{\Theta}_{n}=\mathbf{I}_{p}/p$ we deduce that

$$ \frac{1}{p}{\sf tr}(\big(\widehat{{\bm{\Sigma}}}-z\mathbf{I}_{p}\big)^{-1})\approx\frac{1}{p}{\sf tr}\big(a_{n}{\bm{\Sigma}}-z\mathbf{I}_{p}\big)^{-1} $$

Note that the left hand side is

$$ m_{\widehat{H}_{n}}(z)\xrightarrow{a.s.}m(z) $$

since $\widehat{H}_{n}\xrightarrow{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}$ as proved in Proposition A.2. Thus we deduce that

$$ m(z)=\lim_{n}\frac{1}{p}{\sf tr}\big(a_{n}{\bm{\Sigma}}-z\mathbf{I}_{p}\big)^{-1}=\lim_{n}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{s}\frac{1}{p}\cdot\frac{1}{a_{n}(\delta_{j}+\sigma_{0}^{2})-z}+\frac{p-s}{p}\cdot\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z}\right] $$

Suppose for the sake of contradiction that $\limsup_{n\to\infty}|a_{n}|=+\infty$ and choose a subsequence along which $|a_{n}|\to\infty$ . Then each summand in the right hand side converges to 0 hence the entire right-hand side converges to $0$ along that subsequence. This contradicts the equality since $m(z)$ is finite and nonzero for $z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}_{+}$ . Therefore $\{a_{n}(z)\}_{n}$ must be bounded. By Bolzano-Weierstrass, any subsequence has a further subsequence $a_{n_{k}}\to a$ . Passing to the limit in the equality below, the first $s$ terms are negligible and thus

$$ m(z)=\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a-z}. $$

Consequently, $a$ must equal the unique solution of $m(z)=1/(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a-z)$ , namely

$$ a(z)=\frac{z}{\sigma_{0}^{2}}+\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,m(z)}. $$

Hence, every convergent subsequence of $\{a_{n}(z)\}$ has the same limit $a(z)$ , and therefore we can conclude that $a_{n}(z)\to a(z)$ . The second equality follows from the relation between the Stieltjes transform and the companion Stieltjes transform (Equation (A.2)):

$$ {z\underline{m}(z)+1}=z\left(\underline{m}(z)+\frac{1}{z}\right)=z\left(cm(z)+\frac{c}{z}\right)=zcm(z)+c=1-\frac{z}{\sigma_{0}^{2}}-\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,m(z)}\,, $$

which immediately implies:

$$ -z\underline{m}(z)=\frac{z}{\sigma_{0}^{2}}+\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,m(z)}=a(z)\,. $$

This completes the proof. ∎

#### A.3.2 Proof of Proposition A.5

#### Proof.

Since $\{\bm{v}_{1},\dots,\bm{v}_{s}\}$ is orthonormal, we can extend this set by $p-s$ new vectors $\{\mathfrak{u}_{1},\dots,\mathfrak{u}_{p-s}\}$ to an orthonormal basis of $\mathrm{R}^{p}$ . In particular, we have

$$ \mathbf{I}_{p}=\sum_{j=1}^{s}\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}+\sum_{i=1}^{p-s}\mathfrak{u}_{i}\mathfrak{u}_{i}^{\top} $$

We deduce that ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ is diagonal in this basis

$$ {\bm{\Sigma}}=\sigma_{0}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{p}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}=\left(\sigma_{0}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{p}-\sigma_{0}^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{s}\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}(\delta_{j}+\sigma_{0}^{2})\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}=\sigma_{0}^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{p-s}\mathfrak{u}_{i}\mathfrak{u}_{i}^{\top}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}(\delta_{j}+\sigma_{0}^{2})\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top} $$

and thus

$$ \displaystyle(a_{n}{\bm{\Sigma}}-z\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1} \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{p-s}\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z}\mathfrak{u}_{i}\mathfrak{u}_{i}^{\top}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\frac{1}{a_{n}(\delta_{j}+\sigma_{0}^{2})-z}\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z}\mathbf{I}_{p}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\left(\frac{1}{a_{n}(\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta_{j})-z}-\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z}\right)\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z}\mathbf{I}_{p}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{j}\,a_{n}}{(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z)\bigl(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z+\delta_{j}\,a_{n}\bigr)}\,\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z}\left[\mathbf{I}_{p}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{j}\,a_{n}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z+\delta_{j}\,a_{n}}\,\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\right] $$

This completes the proof. ∎

### A.4 Limiting Probability Measures for One-Spike Covariance Matrix

In this section, we consider a simple one-spike covariance matrix, as this will lay the foundation for analyzing general $s$ -spike covariance matrices. We will establish properties of the limiting spectral distribution for one non-trivial empirical measure. First, let us introduce the notations. Consider the one spike covariance

$$ {\bm{\Sigma}}^{\prime}=\sigma_{0}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{p}+\delta\,\mathfrak{v}_{1}\mathfrak{v}_{1}^{\top}, $$

where $\mathfrak{v}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ is a unit vector. Its eigenvalues are $\mathfrak{d}_{1}^{\prime}=\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta$ and $\mathfrak{d}_{2}^{\prime}=\cdots=\mathfrak{d}_{p}^{\prime}=\sigma_{0}^{2}$ and we can extend $\mathfrak{v}_{1}$ to an orthonormal basis $\{\mathfrak{v}_{1},\dots,\mathfrak{v}_{p}\}$ of $\mathrm{R}^{p}$ . Next, draw $n$ i.i.d. vectors $\bm{x}_{1}^{\prime},\dots,\bm{x}_{n}^{\prime}$ with covariance ${\bm{\Sigma}}^{\prime}$ , and let

$$ \widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}^{\prime}=\frac{{\bm{X}^{\prime}}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\prime}}{n}=\sum_{j=1}^{p}d_{j}^{\prime}\,\bm{w}^{\prime}_{j}\bm{w}_{j}^{\prime\top} $$

be the sample covariance matrix and its spectral decomposition, where $\{d_{1}^{\prime},\dots,d_{p}^{\prime}\}$ and $\{\bm{w}^{\prime}_{1},\dots,\bm{w}^{\prime}_{p}\}$ are its eigenvalues and its corresponding eigenvectors. In this setup, we prove the following lemma.

#### Lemma A.6.

Let ${\bm{\Sigma}}^{\prime}=\sigma_{0}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{p}+\delta\,\mathfrak{v}_{1}\mathfrak{v}_{1}^{\top}$ with $\delta>0$ be a one-spike covariance, where $\mathfrak{v}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ is a unit vector. Using the notation introduced above, define the population ESD of ${\bm{\Sigma}}^{\prime}$ by

$$ \widehat{H}_{n}^{\prime}(x):=\frac{1}{p}\sum_{i=1}^{p}\mathbf{1}\{\mathfrak{d}_{i}^{\prime}\leq x\},\qquad\widehat{F}_{\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{p}\sum_{i=1}^{p}\mathbf{1}\{d_{i}^{\prime}\leq x\} $$

and the two weighted empirical distribution functions

$$ \widehat{G}_{n}^{\prime}(x):=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\bigl\langle\mathfrak{v}_{1},\mathfrak{v}_{i}\bigr\rangle^{2}\,\mathbf{1}\{\mathfrak{d}_{i}^{\prime}\leq x\},\qquad\widehat{B}_{n}^{\prime}(x):=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\bigl\langle\mathfrak{v}_{1},\bm{w}^{\prime}_{i}\bigr\rangle^{2}\,\mathbf{1}\{d_{i}^{\prime}\leq x\}. $$

Then the following statements hold.

- (a) $\widehat{H}_{n}^{\prime}\xrightarrow{d}H^{\prime}:=\mathbf{1}\{\sigma_{0}^{2}\leq x\},$ $\widehat{F}_{\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}^{\prime}}\xrightarrow{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}$ and $\widehat{G}_{n}^{\prime}\xrightarrow{d}G^{\prime}=\mathbf{1}\{\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta\leq x\}.$

- (b) $\widehat{B}_{n}^{\prime}\xrightarrow{d}F_{\delta},$ where $F_{\delta}$ is a probability measure with support contained in

$$ \operatorname{supp}(F_{\delta})\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{c}\cup\{0\}\cup\{x_{\delta}^{\star}\},\qquad x_{\delta}^{\star}=\frac{(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})(\delta+c\sigma_{0}^{2})}{\delta}, $$

and where $\mathcal{S}_{c}=\bigl[\sigma_{0}^{2}(1-\sqrt{c})^{2},\sigma_{0}^{2}(1+\sqrt{c})^{2}\bigr]$ denotes the Marchenko–Pastur bulk.

- (c) The Stieltjes transform of $F_{\delta}$ is $m_{\delta}$ which satisfies

$$ m_{\delta}(z)=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}m(z)}{\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta+\delta z\,m(z)}\qquad z\in\mathbb{C}^{+}. $$

(A.7)

- (d) (i) The measure $F_{\delta}$ is absolutely continuous on $\mathrm{int}(\mathcal{S}_{c})$ with density

$$ f_{\delta}(x)=\frac{c\sigma_{0}^{2}(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})\,f_{\mathrm{MP}}(x)}{c\sigma_{0}^{4}+(c+1)\delta\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta^{2}-\delta x},\qquad x\in\mathrm{int}(\mathcal{S}_{c}). $$

(ii) If $c>1$ , then $F_{\delta}$ has an atom at 0 with mass

$$ F_{\delta}(\{0\})=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}(c-1)}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta}. $$

(iii) If $\delta>\sigma_{0}^{2}\sqrt{c}$ , then $F_{\delta}$ has an atom at $x_{\delta}^{\star}$ with mass

$$ F_{\delta}\bigl(\{x_{\delta}^{\star}\}\bigr)=\frac{\delta^{2}-c\sigma_{0}^{4}}{\delta(\delta+c\sigma_{0}^{2})}. $$

(A.8) In particular, if $c\leq 1$ and $\delta\leq\sigma_{0}^{2}\sqrt{c}$ then $F_{\delta}$ has no atoms.

#### Proof of Lemma A.6(a).

Note that the 1 spike covariance structure is a special case of the $s$ -spike covariance. The first two limits follow now by Proposition A.2. Next, recall that $\{\mathfrak{v}_{1},\dots,\mathfrak{v}_{p}\}$ is an orthonormal basis, so $\langle\mathfrak{v}_{1},\mathfrak{\bm{v}}_{j}\rangle=0$ for $j\neq 1$ so

$$ \widehat{G}_{n}^{\prime}(x)=\mathbf{1}\{\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta\leq x\}, $$

so the sequence does not depend on $n$ . The limit now follows. ∎

The proofs of (b), (c), and (d) are more involved. We group (b) and (c) together since they follow by adapting certain arguments from Lemma 1 and Lemma 3 in [84].

#### A.4.1 Proof of Theorem A.6(b) and (c)

#### Proof.

Using Lemma 1 in [84] for $\widehat{B}_{n}^{\prime}$ and ${\bm{\beta}}^{\star}=\mathfrak{v}_{1}$ we deduce that for any $z\in\mathbb{C}^{+}$ we have

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}m_{\widehat{B}_{n}^{\prime}}(z)=-\frac{1}{z}\int\frac{1}{1+\tau\,\underline{m}(z)}\,dG^{\prime}(\tau) $$

Note that

$$ \displaystyle-\frac{1}{z}\int\frac{1}{1+\tau\,\underline{m}(z)}\,dG^{\prime}(\tau) \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{z}\,\frac{1}{1+(1+\delta)\underline{m}(z)}=\frac{1}{-z\underline{m}(z)(1+\delta)-z} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a(z)-z+\delta\,a(z)}:=m_{\delta}(z) $$

where the last equality is true by Lemma A.4. Using Lemma 3 in [84], $m_{\delta}$ is the Stieltjes transform of a probability measure $F_{\delta}$ whose support satisfies

$$ \mathrm{supp}(F_{\delta})\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{c}\cup\{0\}\cup\{x_{\delta}^{\star}\},\qquad x_{\delta}^{\star}=\frac{(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})(\delta+c\sigma_{0}^{2})}{\delta} $$

∎

#### A.4.2 Proof of Theorem A.6(d)(i)

#### Proof.

For all $E\in\mathcal{S}_{c}$ and $z=E+i\eta$ we have by inversion of the Stieltjes transform

$$ f_{\delta}(E)=\frac{1}{\pi}\lim_{\eta\to 0^{+}}\Im(m_{\delta}(E+i\eta))=\frac{1}{\pi}\lim_{\eta\to 0^{+}}\Im\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}m(E+i\eta)}{\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta+\delta zm(E+i\eta)} $$

Note that $\Im(x/y)=\Im(x\overline{y}/|y|^{2})$ :

$$ \displaystyle f_{\delta}(E) \displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}}{\pi}\lim_{\eta\to 0^{+}}\frac{\Im\bigl(m(z)(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})+\delta\bar{z}|m(z)|^{2}\bigr)}{|\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta+\delta zm(z)|^{2}} \displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}}{\pi}\lim_{\eta\to 0^{+}}\frac{(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})\Im(m(z))-\eta\delta|m(z)|^{2}}{|\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta+\delta zm(z)|^{2}} \displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}}{\pi}\frac{(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})\,\Im(m(E+i0))}{|\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta+\delta E\,m(E+i0)|^{2}} $$

Recall from Equation (A.1) that

$$ m(z)=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}(1-c)-z+\sqrt{(z-a)(z-b)}}{2cz\sigma_{0}^{2}}, $$

where we choose the branch of the square root with a positive imaginary part; thus

$$ m(E+i0)=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}(1-c)-E}{2cE\sigma_{0}^{2}}+i\,\frac{\sqrt{(b-E)(E-a)}}{2cE\sigma_{0}^{2}}. $$

We conclude that for $E$ in the bulk,

$$ \displaystyle f_{\delta}(E) \displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}}{\pi}\cdot\frac{(\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta)\,\dfrac{\sqrt{(b-E)(E-a)}}{2cE\sigma_{0}^{2}}}{\left(\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta+\dfrac{\delta\bigl(\sigma_{0}^{2}(1-c)-E\bigr)}{2c\sigma_{0}^{2}}\right)^{2}+\left(\dfrac{\delta}{2c\sigma_{0}^{2}}\right)^{2}(b-E)(E-a)} \displaystyle=\frac{c\sigma_{0}^{2}(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})\,f_{\mathrm{MP}}(E)}{(\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta)(c\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta)-\delta E}=\frac{c\sigma_{0}^{2}(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})\,f_{\mathrm{MP}}(E)}{c\sigma_{0}^{4}+(1+c)\delta\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta^{2}-\delta E}. $$

∎

#### A.4.3 Proof of Theorem A.6(d)(ii)

#### Proof.

We compute the mass of the atoms. For $c<1$ the MP law has no atom at 0, hence by inversion

$$ \lim_{\eta\to 0^{+}}-i\eta\,m(i\eta)=0 $$

and thus the same holds for $m_{\delta}$ using the definition of $m_{\delta}$ (A.7).

For $c>1$ the MP law has an atom at 0, and we prove that $F_{\delta}$ have the same property.

$$ F_{\delta}(\{0\})=\lim_{\eta\to 0^{+}}-i\eta\,m_{\delta}(i\eta)=\lim_{\eta\to 0^{+}}-i\eta\,\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}m(i\eta)}{\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta+\delta\,i\eta\,m(i\eta)} $$

Note that by the same token $F_{\text{MP}}(\{0\})=1-\frac{1}{c}=\lim_{\eta\to 0^{+}}-i\eta\,m(i\eta)$ thus

$$ F_{\delta}(\{0\})=\frac{1-\frac{1}{c}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta-\delta(1-\frac{1}{c})}=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}(c-1)}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta}. $$

∎

#### A.4.4 Proof of Theorem A.6(d)(iii)

#### Proof.

As stated in Lemma 3 of [84], the mass of the atom of $F_{\delta}$ at $x_{j}^{\star}$ is nonzero if and only if the eigenvalue $\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2}$ is above the BBP phase transition $\tau_{\mathrm{BBP}}$ [69]. It is well known that $\tau_{\mathrm{BBP}}$ is defined as the fixed-point solution to the equation

$$ \left(1+c\int\frac{\tau^{\prime}}{\tau_{\mathrm{BBP}}-\tau^{\prime}}\,dH(\tau^{\prime})\right)\tau_{\mathrm{BBP}}=\sigma_{0}^{2}(1+\sqrt{c})^{2}. $$

See for example Theorem 1.1 in [69] or Equation 19 in [84]. Recall from Theorem A.6(a) that $H^{\prime}(x)=\mathbf{1}\{\sigma_{0}^{2}\leq x\}$ , so the fixed point equation can be simplified to

$$ \tau_{\mathrm{BBP}}=\sigma_{0}^{2}(1+\sqrt{c}). $$

Using Lemma 3 in [84] we can conclude that that if $\delta+1>\tau_{\mathrm{BBP}}$ , or equivalently $\delta>\sqrt{c}$ , the mass of the atom is

$$ F_{\delta}(\{x_{j}^{\star}\})=\frac{1-c\displaystyle\int\left(\frac{\tau^{\prime}}{\delta+1-\tau^{\prime}}\right)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}H^{\prime}(\tau^{\prime})}{1+c\displaystyle\int\frac{\tau^{\prime}}{\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2}-\tau^{\prime}}\,\mathrm{d}H^{\prime}(\tau^{\prime})}. $$

Since $H^{\prime}(x)=\mathbf{1}\{\sigma_{0}^{2}\leq x\}$ .

$$ \int\frac{\tau^{\prime}}{\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2}-\tau^{\prime}}\,dH(\tau^{\prime})=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}}{\delta},\qquad\int\left(\frac{\tau^{\prime}}{\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2}-\tau^{\prime}}\right)^{2}dH(\tau^{\prime})=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{4}}{\delta^{2}}, $$

and substituting into the display above yields

$$ \displaystyle F_{\delta}(\{x_{j}^{\star}\}) \displaystyle=\frac{1-\frac{c\sigma_{0}^{4}}{\delta^{2}}}{1+\frac{c\sigma_{0}^{2}}{\delta}}=\frac{\delta^{2}-c\sigma_{0}^{4}}{\delta(\delta+c\sigma_{0}^{2})}. $$

On the other hand, if $\delta^{2}\leq c\sigma_{0}^{2}$ (equivalently, $\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2}\leq\tau_{\mathrm{BBP}}$ ), there is no outlier atom. This ends the proof. ∎

### A.5 Auxiliary Empirical Measures and Weak Convergence via Stieltjes Transforms

In this section, we introduce three empirical measures that will be useful for deriving limits of general $f$ -estimators. We assume throughout this section that ${\bm{\Sigma}}=\sigma_{0}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{p}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}$ is an $s$ -spike covariance. Consider the spectral decomposition of the sample covariance

$$ \widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}d_{i}\,\bm{w}_{i}\bm{w}_{i}^{\top}, $$

where $d_{1},\dots,d_{p}$ are the eigenvalues and $\bm{w}_{1},\dots,\bm{w}_{p}$ are the corresponding eigenvectors. Define

$$ \displaystyle\widehat{B}_{n}(x) \displaystyle:=\frac{1}{\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{p}\langle{\bm{\beta}}_{0},\bm{w}_{i}\rangle^{2}\,\mathbf{1}\{d_{i}\leq x\}, \displaystyle\widehat{C}_{n}^{\,j}(x) \displaystyle:=\frac{1}{{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j}}\sum_{i=1}^{p}\langle{\bm{\beta}}_{0},\bm{w}_{i}\rangle\,\langle\bm{v}_{j},\bm{w}_{i}\rangle\,\mathbf{1}\{d_{i}\leq x\}, \displaystyle\widehat{D}_{n}^{\,j}(x) \displaystyle:=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\langle\bm{v}_{j},\bm{w}_{i}\rangle^{2}\,\mathbf{1}\{d_{i}\leq x\}, $$

for each spike direction $\bm{v}_{j}$ , $j\in\{1,\dots,s\}$ . The following three lemmas allow us to represent these empirical measures in terms of specific spiked measures $F_{\delta}$ that we have introduced in Section A.6.

#### Lemma A.7.

If ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ is an $s$ -spike covariance and $\alpha_{j}\neq 0$ for all $j=1,2\dots,s$ then

$$ \widehat{B}_{n}\xrightarrow{d}F_{\alpha}:=\omega_{0}F_{\mathrm{MP}}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\omega_{j}F_{\delta_{j}} $$

where

$$ \omega_{0}=\frac{r^{2}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\alpha_{j}^{2}}{r^{2}}\qquad\omega_{j}=\frac{\alpha_{j}^{2}}{r^{2}} $$

are positive weights that sum to 1.

The other two measures that depend on $j$ converge weakly to the same probability measure, as described in the two lemmas below.

#### Lemma A.8.

Fix $j\in\{1,2\dots,s\}$ . If ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ is an $s$ -spike covariance and $\alpha_{j}\neq 0$ then $\widehat{C}_{n}^{j}(x)\xrightarrow{}F_{\delta_{j}}$ vaguely.

#### Lemma A.9.

Fix $j\in\{1,2\dots,s\}$ . If ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ is an $s$ -spike covariance then $\widehat{D}_{n}^{j}(x)\xrightarrow{d}F_{\delta_{j}}$ .

The proofs for Lemma A.7 and Lemma A.9 are standard and use the fact that for any sequence of random probability measures $\mu_{n}$ whenever $m_{\mu_{n}}(z)\to m(z)$ point-wise on $\mathbb{C}^{+}$ and $m$ is the Stieltjes transform of a probability measure $\mu$ we have $\mu_{n}\xrightarrow{d}\mu$ in weak topology. For Lemma A.8, we will use a more general result that vague convergence holds for signed measures that are uniformly bounded in total variation, using Theorem B.9 in [85].

#### A.5.1 Proof of Lemma A.7

Note that $\widehat{B}_{n}$ is a probability distribution since the total mass is 1 and all weights are non-negative. By definition, we have

$$ \displaystyle m_{\widehat{B}_{n}}(z) \displaystyle=\int\frac{1}{x-z}\,d\widehat{B}_{n}(x)=\frac{1}{\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{\langle{\bm{\beta}}_{0},\bm{w}_{i}\rangle^{2}}{d_{i}-z}=\frac{{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}-z\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}}{\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}}. $$

To justify the deterministic equivalent for this quadratic form, we apply the deterministic equivalent property with $\bm{\Theta}_{n}={\bm{\beta}}_{0}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}$ , which is bounded in trace norm since $\|\bm{\Theta}_{n}\|_{1}={\sf tr}(\bm{\Theta}_{n})=\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}$ . As before, we write $x_{n}\approx y_{n}$ if $x_{n}-y_{n}\to 0$ almost surely. Using the deterministic equivalent (A.4) and Proposition A.5 we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}-z\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}}{\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}}\;\approx\;\frac{1}{\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}}\,{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z}\left[\mathbf{I}_{p}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{j}\,a_{n}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z+\delta_{j}\,a_{n}}\,\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\right]{\bm{\beta}}_{0}, $$

where the spike eigenvectors satisfy $\|\bm{v}_{j}\|_{2}=1$ . Expanding the quadratic form gives

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}}\,{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}a_{n}-z}\left[\mathbf{I}_{p}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{j}\,a_{n}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z+\delta_{j}\,a_{n}}\,\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\right]{\bm{\beta}}_{0} \displaystyle\qquad=\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z}\cdot\frac{1}{\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}}\left[\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{j}\,a_{n}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z+\delta_{j}\,a_{n}}\,({\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j})^{2}\right]. $$

Using

$$ \frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z}\cdot\frac{\delta_{j}\,a_{n}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z+\delta_{j}\,a_{n}}=\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z}-\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z+\delta_{j}\,a_{n}}, $$

we obtain

$$ \displaystyle m_{\widehat{B}_{n}}(z)\;\approx\;\left(1-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\frac{({\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j})^{2}}{\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}}\right)\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\frac{({\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j})^{2}}{\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z+\delta_{j}\,a_{n}}. $$

Since $a_{n}(z)\to a(z)$ pointwise, we get the pointwise limit

$$ \displaystyle m_{\widehat{B}_{n}}(z)\ \xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\ \left(1-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\alpha_{j}^{2}}{r^{2}}\right)m(z)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\alpha_{j}^{2}}{r^{2}}\,m_{\delta_{j}}(z). $$

Since $\widehat{B}_{n}$ is a probability measure, we deduce that $\widehat{B}_{n}$ converges weakly to the (unique) probability measure with the above Stieltjes transform. Note that this is nothing else but a finite mixture of $F_{\mathrm{MP}}$ , and the $F_{\delta}$ ’s:

$$ F_{\alpha}:=\omega_{0}F_{\mathrm{MP}}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\omega_{j}F_{\delta_{j}}, $$

where

$$ \omega_{0}=1-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\alpha_{j}^{2}}{r^{2}}\qquad\omega_{j}=\frac{\alpha_{j}^{2}}{r^{2}} $$

are weights that sum to 1. By definition $\omega_{j}>0$ for all $j\geq 1$ . To show $\omega_{0}>0$ recall equation (A.6),

$$ \mathbf{I}_{p}=\sum_{j=1}^{s}\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}+\sum_{i=1}^{p-s}\mathfrak{u}_{i}\mathfrak{u}_{i}^{\top}, $$

and note that if we multiply both sides by ${\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}$ to the left and ${\bm{\beta}}_{0}$ to the right we have

$$ \|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|^{2}_{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{s}({\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j})^{2}+\|\widetilde{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}, $$

which proves that $\omega_{0}>0$ after sending $n\to\infty$ . We conclude that $\widehat{B}_{n}\xrightarrow{d}F_{\alpha}$ and $F_{\alpha}$ is a probability measure.

#### A.5.2 Proof of Lemma A.8

Fix $1\leq j\leq s$ . This measure has total mass $1$ but is not necessarily nonnegative, so convergence requires additional care. We start with the following uniform bound on the total variation norm.

#### Lemma A.10.

Fix $j$ such that ${\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j}\neq 0$ . Then

$$ \|\widehat{C}_{n}^{\,j}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\;\leq\;\frac{\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}}{|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j}|}. $$

In particular, $\{\widehat{C}_{n}^{\,j}\}_{n}$ is uniformly bounded in total variation.

#### Proof.

For any $x$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\widehat{C}_{n}^{\,j}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j}|}\sum_{i=1}^{p}|\langle{\bm{\beta}}_{0},\bm{w}_{i}\rangle|\,|\langle\bm{v}_{j},\bm{w}_{i}\rangle|\;\leq\;\frac{1}{|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j}|}\,\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{p}\langle{\bm{\beta}}_{0},\bm{w}_{i}\rangle^{2}}\,\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{p}\langle\bm{v}_{j},\bm{w}_{i}\rangle^{2}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j}|}\,\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}\,\|\bm{v}_{j}\|_{2}=\frac{\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}}{|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j}|}, $$

using Cauchy–Schwarz and the orthonormality of $\{\bm{w}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{p}$ . ∎

We return now to the main proof. As above, we apply the deterministic equivalent (A.4) property and Proposition A.5

$$ {\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}-z\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}v={\sf tr}((\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}-z\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}\bm{\Theta}_{n}) $$

with $\bm{\Theta}_{n}=\bm{v}_{j}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}$ , which is bounded in trace norm since $\|\bm{v}_{j}\|_{2}=1$ and $\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}$ are bounded. Using the equivalent from A.3,

$$ \displaystyle m_{\widehat{C}_{n}^{j}}(z)=\frac{{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}-z\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}\bm{v}_{j}}{{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j}}\;\approx\;\frac{1}{{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j}}\,{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\frac{1}{a_{n}-z}\left[\mathbf{I}_{p}-\sum_{i=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{i}\,a_{n}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z+\delta_{i}\,a_{n}}\,v_{i}v_{i}^{\top}\right]\bm{v}_{j}. $$

Expanding using $\|\bm{v}_{j}\|_{2}=1$ and $\bm{v}_{j}\perp v_{i}$ for all $i\neq j$ yields

$$ m_{\widehat{C}_{n}^{j}}(z)\ \approx\ \frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z+\delta\,a_{n}}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad m_{\widehat{C}_{n}^{j}}(z)\ \xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\ \frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a-z+\delta\,a}=m_{\delta}(z). $$

Hence, by Theorem B.9 in [85], $\widehat{C}_{n}^{j}$ converges vaguely to $F_{\delta_{j}}$ , the (unique) probability measure with Stieltjes transform $m_{\delta_{j}}$ .

#### A.5.3 Proof of Lemma A.9

Note that $\widehat{D}_{n}^{\,j}$ is a probability measure since $\widehat{D}_{n}^{\,j}(\infty)=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\langle\bm{v}_{j},\bm{w}_{i}\rangle^{2}=\|\bm{v}_{j}\|_{2}^{2}=1$ . Its Stieltjes transform is

$$ \displaystyle m_{\widehat{D}_{n}^{\,j}}(z) \displaystyle:=\int\frac{1}{x-z}\,d\widehat{D}_{n}^{\,j}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{\langle\bm{v}_{j},\bm{w}_{i}\rangle^{2}}{d_{i}-z}=\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}-z\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}\bm{v}_{j}. $$

Mutatis mutandis, we use the deterministic equivalent property with $\bm{\Theta}_{n}=\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top},$ which is bounded in trace norm since $\|\bm{\Theta}_{n}\|_{1}={\sf tr}(\bm{\Theta}_{n})=\|\bm{v}_{j}\|_{2}^{2}=1$ . Using the deterministic equivalent (A.4) property and Proposition A.5

$$ \displaystyle\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}-z\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}\bm{v}_{j}\;\approx\;\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\frac{1}{a_{n}-z}\left[\mathbf{I}_{p}-\sum_{\ell=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{\ell}a_{n}}{a_{n}-z+\delta_{\ell}a_{n}}\,\bm{v}_{\ell}\bm{v}_{\ell}^{\top}\right]\bm{v}_{j}. $$

Expanding the quadratic form and using orthonormality $\bm{v}_{\ell}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j}=\mathbf{1}\{\ell=j\}$ gives

$$ \displaystyle\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z}\left[\mathbf{I}_{p}-\sum_{\ell=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{\ell}\,a_{n}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z+\delta_{\ell}\,a_{n}}\,\bm{v}_{\ell}\bm{v}_{\ell}^{\top}\right]\bm{v}_{j} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z}\left[1-\frac{\delta_{j}\,a_{n}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z+\delta_{j}\,a_{n}}\right] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n}-z+\delta_{j}\,a_{n}} \displaystyle=m_{\delta_{j}}(z). $$

Hence, $m_{\widehat{D}_{n}^{\,j}}(z)\ \xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\ m_{\delta_{j}}(z)$ and because $\widehat{D}_{n}^{\,j}$ is a probability measure, we can deduce weak convergence of the underlying measures $\widehat{D}_{n}^{\,j}\ \xrightarrow{d}\ F_{\delta_{j}}$ .

### A.6 Radon-Nikodym Derivatives

In this section, we relate all the (limiting) probability measures we defined in the previous sections: $F_{\mathrm{MP}},F_{\delta}$ via their Radon-Nikodym derivative w.r.t. $F_{\alpha}$ . For all $j\in\{1,2,\dots s\}$ let

$$ x^{\star}_{j}=\frac{(\delta_{j}+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,)(\delta_{j}+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,)}{\delta_{j}} $$

be the possible atom of $F_{\delta_{j}}$ if $\delta_{j}^{2}>c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,$ (see equation (A.8)). Recall that $\mathcal{S}_{c}=[\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1-\sqrt{c})^{2},\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1+\sqrt{c})^{2}]$ is the bulk of the $F_{\mathrm{MP}}$ distribution. By Lemma A.6(d)(i) we can deduce that this is also the bulk of $F_{\delta_{j}}$ for all $j$ . Since $F_{\alpha}$ is just a mixture of the previous distributions, it must have the same bulk. We start by proving a basic lemma that relates $F_{\delta}$ and $F_{\mathrm{MP}}$ .

#### Lemma A.11.

Let $\delta>0$ . Then $F_{\mathrm{MP}}\ll F_{\delta}$ and moreover

$$ \nu_{\delta}(x):=\frac{\mathrm{d}F_{\text{MP}}(x)}{\mathrm{d}F_{\delta}(x)}=\frac{(\delta+c\sigma_{0}^{2})(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})-\delta x}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,)}=\frac{\delta(x_{\delta}^{\star}-x)}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,)}, $$

for $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}\cup\{0\}\cup\{x_{\delta}^{\star}\}$ is a Radon-Nikodym derivative of $F_{\text{MP}}$ w.r.t. $F_{\delta}$ . Equivalently, we have

$$ \int\phi\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}=\int\phi\,\nu_{\delta}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta} $$

for all test functions $\phi$ for which both integrals are finite.

Next, we assume a minimal condition on the spike strengths to avoid possible degeneracy. All results proved in this paper generalize to these edge cases via minimal changes.

#### Lemma A.12.

If Assumption 2.3(1) holds, then the points $\{x_{j}^{\star}\}_{j=1}^{s}$ are distinct and at positive distance to the right of the bulk $\mathcal{S}_{c}$ .

Next, we introduce some notations. Recall from Lemma A.11 that for all $\delta_{j}>0$ we can define

$$ \nu_{j}(x):=\frac{\mathrm{d}F_{\text{MP}}(x)}{\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j}}(x)}=\frac{\delta_{j}(x_{j}^{\star}-x)}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}(\delta_{j}+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,)}. $$

Further, define

$$ \displaystyle\nu_{-i}(x):=\prod_{j\neq i}\nu_{j}(x)\qquad\qquad\nu(x):=\prod_{j}\nu_{j}(x). $$

#### Remark A.13.

The polynomials $\nu_{-i}(x)$ act as Lagrange interpolation polynomials since $\nu_{j}(x_{i}^{\star})=0$ if and only if $i=j$ . It will become clear why this is instrumental in Appendix D.

Finally, we combine Lemma A.11 with the assumptions of Lemma A.12 to find the Radon-Nikodym derivatives of $F_{\mathrm{MP}}$ and the $F_{\delta_{j}}$ ’s w.r.t. $F_{\alpha}$ .

#### Lemma A.14.

Let ${\bm{\Sigma}}=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\mathbf{I}_{p}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}$ and assume that the conditions from Lemma A.12 hold. Also, assume that $\omega_{j}\neq 0$ for all $j\in\{1,2,\dots,s\}$ . Then $F_{\mathrm{MP}}\ll{F_{\alpha}}$ and for all $j\in\{1,2,\dots,s\}$ we have $F_{{\delta_{j}}}\ll{F_{\alpha}}.$ Moreover,

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j}}}{\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}}:=\mu_{j}(x):=\frac{\nu_{-j}(x)}{\omega_{0}\nu(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}\nu_{-i}(x)} $$

and

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}}{\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}}:=\mu_{0}(x):=\frac{\nu(x)}{\omega_{0}\nu(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}\nu_{-i}(x)}, $$

for all $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}$ .

#### A.6.1 Proof of Lemma A.11

#### Proof.

Note that by equation (A.13), it is enough to define the Radon–Nikodym derivative only on $\operatorname{supp}(F_{\delta})\cup\operatorname{supp}(F_{\mathrm{MP}})$ . By Lemma A.6(b), this is $\operatorname{supp}(F_{\delta})\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{c}\cup\{0\}\cup\{x_{\delta}^{\star}\}$ . We want to show that $\nu_{\delta}$ satisfies

$$ \int\phi\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}=\int\phi\,\nu_{\delta}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta} $$

for all test functions $\phi$ for which both integrals are finite. Write the two integrals by separating the absolutely continuous and atomic parts:

$$ \int\phi\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}=\int_{\mathcal{S}_{c}}\phi(x)\,f_{\mathrm{MP}}(x)\,dx+\phi(0)\,F_{\mathrm{MP}}(\{0\}), $$

and

$$ \int\phi\,\nu_{\delta}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta}=\int_{\mathcal{S}_{c}}\phi(x)\,\nu_{\delta}(x)\,f_{\delta}(x)\,dx+\phi(0)\,\nu_{\delta}(0)\,F_{\delta}(\{0\})+\phi(x_{\delta}^{\star})\,\nu_{\delta}(x_{\delta}^{\star})\,F_{\delta}(\{x_{\delta}^{\star}\}), $$

On $\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{S}_{c})$ , Lemma A.6(d)(i) gives

$$ f_{\delta}(x)=\frac{c\sigma_{0}^{2}(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})\,f_{\mathrm{MP}}(x)}{c\sigma_{0}^{4}+(c+1)\delta\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta^{2}-\delta x},\qquad x\in\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{S}_{c}), $$

hence

$$ \frac{f_{\mathrm{MP}}(x)}{f_{\delta}(x)}=\frac{(\delta+c\sigma_{0}^{2})(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})-\delta x}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,)}=:\nu_{\delta}(x),\qquad x\in\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{S}_{c}). $$

Therefore, for this choice,

$$ \int_{\mathcal{S}_{c}}\phi(x)\,\nu_{\delta}(x)\,f_{\delta}(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathcal{S}_{c}}\phi(x)\,f_{\mathrm{MP}}(x)\,dx. $$

It remains to match the contributions from the atoms. If $c\leq 1$ , then $F_{\delta}(\{0\})=F_{\mathrm{MP}}(\{0\})=0$ (Lemma A.6(d)(ii)), so this holds regardless of the value of $\nu_{\delta}(0)$ . If $c>1$ , Lemma A.6(d)(ii) yields $F_{\delta}(\{0\})=\sigma_{0}^{2}(c-1)/(c\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta)>0$ , and $F_{\mathrm{MP}}(\{0\})=(c-1)/c$ so we need

$$ \frac{F_{\mathrm{MP}}(\{0\})}{F_{\delta}(\{0\})}=\frac{(c-1)/c}{\sigma_{0}^{2}(c-1)/(c\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta)}=\frac{c\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}} $$

which matches $\nu_{\delta}(0)$ as defined in the statement. Finally, $F_{\mathrm{MP}}$ has no atom at $x_{\delta}^{\star}$ , so we must have $\nu_{\delta}(x_{\delta}^{\star})\,F_{\delta}(\{x_{\delta}^{\star}\})=0$ . By the formula for $\nu_{\delta}$ ,

$$ \nu_{\delta}(x_{\delta}^{\star})=\frac{\delta(x_{\delta}^{\star}-x_{\delta}^{\star})}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})}=0, $$

so this holds whether or not $F_{\delta}$ has an atom at $x_{\delta}^{\star}$ . Putting the continuous and atomic parts together, we obtain

$$ \int\phi\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}=\int\phi\,\nu_{\delta}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta} $$

for all test functions $\phi$ for which both integrals are finite. Hence $F_{\mathrm{MP}}\ll F_{\delta}$ and $\nu_{\delta}=\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}/\mathrm{d}F_{\delta}$ on $\operatorname{supp}(F_{\delta})$ . ∎

#### A.6.2 Proof of Lemma A.12

#### Proof.

The proof is purely algebraic. Define $\varphi:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ by

$$ \varphi(x):=\frac{(x+\sigma_{0}^{2})(x+c\sigma_{0}^{2})}{x}=x+\frac{c\sigma_{0}^{4}}{x}+\sigma_{0}^{2}+c\sigma_{0}^{2}. $$

Then

$$ \varphi^{\prime}(x)=1-\frac{c\sigma_{0}^{4}}{x^{2}},\qquad\varphi^{\prime\prime}(x)=\frac{2c\sigma_{0}^{4}}{x^{3}}>0. $$

Hence $\varphi^{\prime}$ vanishes only at $x=\sqrt{c}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,$ , and since $\varphi^{\prime\prime}(\sqrt{c}\,\sigma_{0}^{2})>0$ , the point $x=\sqrt{c}\,\sigma_{0}^{2}\,$ is the unique global minimizer of $\varphi$ on $(0,\infty)$ . In particular, $\varphi$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\sqrt{c}\,\sigma_{0}^{2})$ and strictly increasing on $(\sqrt{c}\,\sigma_{0}^{2},\infty)$ , and

$$ \min_{x>0}\varphi(x)=\varphi(\sqrt{c}\,\sigma_{0}^{2}\,)=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1+\sqrt{c})^{2}. $$

Note that by definition $x_{j}^{\star}=\varphi(\delta_{j})$ , so we obtain $x_{j}^{\star}\geq\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1+\sqrt{c})^{2},$ with strict inequality whenever $\delta_{j}\neq\sqrt{c}\sigma_{0}^{2}$ . By assumption, $\delta_{j}^{2}\neq c$ for all $j$ , hence $\delta_{j}\neq\sqrt{c}$ and therefore

$$ x_{j}^{\star}>\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1+\sqrt{c})^{2}, $$

i.e. each $x_{j}^{\star}$ lies strictly to the right of the bulk $\mathcal{S}_{c}=[\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1-\sqrt{c})^{2},\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1+\sqrt{c})^{2}]$ .

Next we show that the points $\{x_{j}^{\star}\}_{j=1}^{s}$ are distinct. Suppose $\varphi(\delta_{i})=\varphi(\delta_{j})$ . Then

$$ \delta_{i}+\frac{c\sigma_{0}^{4}}{\delta_{i}}=\delta_{j}+\frac{c\sigma_{0}^{4}}{\delta_{j}}\iff(\delta_{i}-\delta_{j})\left(1-\frac{c\sigma_{0}^{4}}{\delta_{i}\delta_{j}}\right)=0. $$

Thus either $\delta_{i}=\delta_{j}$ or $\delta_{i}\delta_{j}=c\sigma_{0}^{4}\,$ . The assumptions $\delta_{i}\neq\delta_{j}$ for $i\neq j$ and $\delta_{i}\delta_{j}\neq c\sigma_{0}^{4}$ for all $i,j$ rule out both possibilities unless $i=j$ . Hence the values $x_{j}^{\star}=\varphi(\delta_{j})$ are pairwise distinct. ∎

#### A.6.3 Proof of Lemma A.14

#### Proof.

The proof is very similar to that of Lemma A.11, i.e., it is enough to show that in the bulk $\mu_{j}$ is the ratio of the densities of $F_{\delta_{j}}$ and $F_{\alpha}$ , and the ratio of the masses of the atoms also matches the Radon-Nikodym derivative. Recall from Lemma A.12 that all $x_{j}^{\star}$ are distinct and $x_{j}^{\star}>\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1+\sqrt{c})^{2}$ . In particular, for all $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}$ we have $x_{j}^{\star}>\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1+\sqrt{c})^{2}\geq x$ . Furthermore, from Lemma A.11 we know that

$$ \nu_{j}(x)=\frac{\delta(x_{j}^{\star}-x)}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,)}, $$

so $\nu_{j}(x)>0$ for all $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}$ . As a consequence $\mu_{j}$ and $\mu_{0}$ are well-defined and positive for all $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}$ . Moreover, note that by definition

$$ \nu_{j}(0)=\frac{\delta x_{j}^{\star}}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,)}>0, $$

so $\mu_{j}$ and $\mu_{0}$ are also well-defined at $x=0$ .

Fix now $j\in\{1,2,\dots s\}$ . We prove that $\mu_{j}$ is a valid Radon-Nikodym derivative for $F_{\delta_{j}}$ w.r.t. $F_{\alpha}$ . Recall that

$$ F_{\alpha}=\omega_{0}F_{\mathrm{MP}}+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}F_{\delta_{i}}. $$

We start with the density for $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}$ . By the formula above,

$$ f_{\alpha}(x)=\omega_{0}f_{\mathrm{MP}}(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}f_{\delta_{i}}(x). $$

By Lemma A.11, we know that $f_{\mathrm{MP}}(x)=\nu_{i}(x)f_{\delta_{i}}(x)$ for all $i$ so in particular for all $i$ we have

$$ f_{\delta_{i}}(x)=\frac{f_{\mathrm{MP}}(x)}{\nu_{i}(x)}=\frac{\nu_{j}(x)f_{\delta_{j}}(x)}{\nu_{i}(x)}, $$

so plugging this back in equation (A.16) gives

$$ f_{\alpha}(x)=\omega_{0}\nu_{j}(x)f_{\delta_{j}}(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}\frac{\nu_{j}(x)f_{\delta_{j}}(x)}{\nu_{i}(x)}. $$

Rearranging this yields that

$$ \frac{f_{\delta_{j}}(x)}{f_{\alpha}(x)}=\frac{1}{\omega_{0}\nu_{j}(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}\frac{\nu_{j}(x)}{\nu_{i}(x)}}=\mu_{j}(x), $$

where the last equality follows by multiplying both the denominator and numerator by $\nu_{-j}(x)$ . Thus, $\mu_{j}(x)$ is matches the ratio in the bulk $\mathcal{S}_{c}$ .

Next, we check the ratio at the possible atom at $x=0$ . By equation (A.15) we deduce that

$$ F_{\alpha}(\{0\})=\omega_{0}F_{\mathrm{MP}}(\{0\})+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{j}F_{\delta_{j}}(\{0\}). $$

By Lemma A.11, we know that $F_{\mathrm{MP}}(\{0\})=\nu_{i}(0)F_{\delta_{i}}(\{0\})$ for all $i$ so in particular for all $i$ we have

$$ F_{\delta_{i}}(\{0\})=\frac{F_{\mathrm{MP}}(\{0\})}{\nu_{i}(0)}=\frac{\nu_{j}(0)F_{\delta_{j}}(\{0\})}{\nu_{i}(0)}, $$

so plugging this back in the equation above gives

$$ F_{\alpha}(\{0\})=\omega_{0}\nu_{j}(0)F_{\delta_{j}}(\{0\})+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}\frac{\nu_{j}(0)F_{\delta_{i}}(\{0\})}{\nu_{i}(0)}. $$

Rearranging this yields that

$$ \frac{F_{\delta_{j}}(\{0\})}{F_{\alpha}(\{0\})}=\frac{1}{\omega_{0}\nu_{j}(0)+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}\frac{\nu_{j}(0)}{\nu_{i}(0)}}=\mu_{j}(0), $$

where the last equality follows by multiplying both the denominator and numerator by $\nu_{-j}(0)$ . Thus, $\mu_{j}(0)$ is matches the ratio in the bulk $\mathcal{S}_{c}$ .

Next, we check the ratio at the other possible atoms of $F_{\alpha}$ , i.e. $\{x_{1}^{\star},\dots,x_{s}^{\star}\}$ . For $i\neq j$ , $F_{\delta_{j}}$ has no atom at $x_{i}^{\star}$ so we need to check that $\mu_{j}(x_{i}^{\star})=0$ . This is true since $\nu_{-j}(x_{i}^{\star})=0$ if and only if $i\neq j$ .

Finally, we need to check the atom at $x_{j}^{\star}$ . Using equation (A.15) gives

$$ F_{\alpha}(\{x_{j}^{\star}\})=\omega_{j}F_{\delta_{j}}(\{x_{j}^{\star}\}). $$

If the mass is non-zero, then the ratio is also given by $\mu_{j}(x_{j}^{\star})$ as

$$ \mu_{j}(x_{j}^{\star})=\frac{\nu_{-j}(x_{j}^{\star})}{\omega_{0}\nu(x_{j}^{\star})+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}\nu_{-i}(x_{j}^{\star})}=\frac{\nu_{-j}(x_{j}^{\star})}{\omega_{j}\nu_{-j}(x_{j}^{\star})}=\frac{1}{\omega_{j}}=\frac{F_{\delta_{j}}(\{x_{j}^{\star}\})}{F_{\alpha}(\{x_{j}^{\star}\})}, $$

where we used $\omega_{j}\neq 0$ and $\nu_{-j}(x_{j}^{\star})\neq 0$ . We conclude that $\mu_{j}$ is a valid Radon-Nikodym derivative for $F_{\delta_{j}}$ w.r.t. $F_{\alpha}$ . Mutatis mutandis, $\mu_{0}$ is a valid Radon-Nikodym derivative for $F_{\mathrm{MP}}$ w.r.t. $F_{\alpha}$ . ∎

### A.7 Convergence under Weak/Vague Topology

In this section, we prove the following technical Lemma that allows us to compute limits of general test functions $\phi\in\mathcal{F}$ using only weak/vague convergence.

#### Lemma A.15.

Let ${\phi}\in\mathcal{F}$ be a test function. Then

$$ \int\phi\,\mathrm{d}\widehat{B}_{n}\ \xrightarrow{a.s.}\ \int\phi\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}. $$

Similar results hold for $F_{\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}}$ , $\widehat{C}_{n}^{\,j}$ and $\widehat{D}_{n}^{\,j}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $s^{+}$ be the number of spikes above the BBP threshold. Using the results in [68], we infer that

$$ \displaystyle d_{j}\xrightarrow{a.s.}x_{j}^{\star},\qquad d_{s^{+}+1}\xrightarrow{a.s.}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1+\sqrt{c})^{2},\qquad d_{\min\{n,p\}}\xrightarrow{a.s.}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1-\sqrt{c})^{2}. $$

Since $s^{+}\leq s$ is finite, there exists an event $\Omega_{0}$ with $\mathbb{P}(\Omega_{0})=1$ on which all the above convergences hold simultaneously. Fix $\eta$ small enough so that $\phi$ is continuous on $S_{\eta}:=\{x:\mathrm{dist}(x,\mathcal{S}^{+}_{c})\leq\eta\}$ . By the convergences above, there exists $N(\omega)$ such that for all $n\geq N(\omega)$ ,

$$ d_{j}(n,\omega)\in(x_{j}^{\star}-\eta,\ x_{j}^{\star}+\eta)\quad\text{for }j\leq s^{+}, $$

and

$$ d_{s^{+}+1}(n,\omega)\leq\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1+\sqrt{c})^{2}+\eta,\qquad d_{p}(n,\omega)\geq\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1-\sqrt{c})^{2}-\eta\ \ \text{if }c<1, $$

while if $c\geq 1$ then the smallest eigenvalues lie in $[0,\eta]$ and the nonzero eigenvalues lie above $\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(1-\sqrt{c})^{2}-\eta$ . In particular, for all $n\geq N(\omega)$ ,

$$ \{d_{1}(n,\omega),\dots,d_{p}(n,\omega)\}\ \subset\ S_{\eta}. $$

Since the restriction of $\phi$ to $S_{\eta}$ is bounded and continuous, we can choose a compactly supported continuous function $g\in C_{c}(\mathbb{R})$ such that

$$ \psi(x)=\phi(x)\quad\text{for all }x\in S_{\eta}. $$

For $n\geq N(\omega)$ we then have, because $\widehat{B}_{n}$ is supported on the eigenvalues $\{d_{i}\}_{i=1}^{p}\subset S_{\eta}$ ,

$$ \int\phi\,\mathrm{d}\widehat{B}_{n}(\omega)=\int\psi\,\mathrm{d}\widehat{B}_{n}(\omega). $$

Moreover, the support of $F_{\alpha}$ is contained in $\mathcal{S}^{+}_{c}$ , hence also in $S_{\eta}$ , so

$$ \int\phi\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}=\int\psi\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}. $$

Finally, we already know that $\widehat{B}_{n}\xrightarrow{d}F_{\alpha}$ almost surely, on a set $\Omega_{0}^{\prime}$ of probability 1. Since $\psi\in C_{c}(\mathbb{R})$ , weak/vague convergence implies

$$ \int\psi\,\mathrm{d}\widehat{B}_{n}(\omega)\ \xrightarrow{}\ \int\psi\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(\omega). $$

Combining the equalities with $\psi$ yields

$$ \int\phi\,\mathrm{d}\widehat{B}_{n}\ \xrightarrow{a.s.}\ \int\phi\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha} $$

on $\Omega_{0}\cap\Omega_{0}^{\prime}$ , which happens with probability 1, as claimed. The same argument applies to $F_{\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}}$ , $\widehat{C}_{n}^{\,j}$ and $\widehat{D}_{n}^{\,j}$ since they are measures supported on $\{d_{i}\}_{i=1}^{p}$ . ∎

### A.8 Concentration Properties

We collect here two standard concentration results used throughout the proofs. Both are adapted from [73].

#### Lemma A.16.

([73], Lemma S.4.1) Suppose ${\bm{\varepsilon}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ satisfies Assumption 2.1, and let $\{\bm{a}_{n}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a sequence of random vectors independent of ${\bm{\varepsilon}}$ with $\limsup_{n}\|\bm{a}_{n}\|^{2}/n<\infty$ almost surely. Then, as $n\to\infty$

$$ \frac{\bm{a}_{n}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}}{n}\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}0. $$

#### Lemma A.17.

([73], Lemma S.4.2) Suppose ${\bm{\varepsilon}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ satisfies Assumption 2.1, and let $\{\bm{A}_{n}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be a sequence of random matrices independent of ${\bm{\varepsilon}}$ with $\limsup_{n}\|\bm{A}_{n}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty$ . Then, as $n\to\infty$

$$ \frac{{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{\top}\bm{A}_{n}{\bm{\varepsilon}}}{n}-\frac{\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}{\sf tr}(\bm{A}_{n})}{n}\xrightarrow{a.s.}0. $$

## Appendix B Characterization of $f^{\mathrm{pred}}_{\ast}$ - Proof of Theorem 3.1

### B.1 Proof of Theorem 3.1

Using the tools introduced in Appendix A, we can provide an exact formula for $\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f;c)$ for all functions $f\in\mathcal{F}$ .

#### Lemma B.1.

For any $f\in\mathcal{F}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f;c)\,\,\overset{a.s.}{=}\,\mathcal{B}_{f}^{*}+\mathcal{V}_{f}^{*}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{f}^{*} \displaystyle:=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\int(1-xf(x))^{2}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\left(\int(1-xf(x))\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j}}(x)\right)^{2}, \displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{f}^{*} \displaystyle:=c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\int xf^{2}(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}(x). $$

The goal now is to optimize $\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f;c)$ with respect to $f$ . Optimizing $\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f;c)$ in the anisotropic case requires careful analysis, as it is a nonlinear functional of $f$ and the integrals are with respect to different measures. The key idea is to rewrite this as an optimization problem in a specific Hilbert Space. Let us introduce the following notations

$$ w(x):=\begin{cases}\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}x+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\,\mu_{0}(x)&\text{for }x\in\mathcal{S}^{+}_{c}\\
0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases},\quad g(x):=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\,\mu_{j}(x)}{w(x)},&\text{for }x\in\mathcal{S}^{+}_{c}\\
0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}, $$

$$ h_{j}(x):=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\mu_{j}(x)}{w(x)},&\text{for }x\in\mathcal{S}^{+}_{c}\\
0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\qquad\qquad\text{for }j\in\{0,1,\dots,s\}\,, $$

where we recall the Radon-Nikodym derivatives $\mu_{j}$ from Lemma A.14. Note that $w(x)>0$ for all $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}$ , because at the non-zero atoms $\mu_{0}(x_{j}^{\star})=\omega_{j}^{-1}>0$ and $\mu_{0}(0)>0$ . The bulk positivity is trivial. In the rest of the analysis, we use the notation $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{w}$ to denote the $xw(x)$ -weighted $L_{2}(F_{\alpha})$ inner product, i.e.

$$ \langle\phi,\psi\rangle_{w}=\int\phi(x)\psi(x)xw(x)\ \mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x). $$

Using these notations, the following two lemmas characterize the optimizer of $\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f;c)$ :

#### Lemma B.2.

Recall the definition of $\mathcal{F}$ from Assumption 2.5. Define the linear operator $\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{F}\to\mathcal{F}$ by

$$ \mathcal{A}f=f+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\langle f,h_{j}\rangle_{w}\,h_{j}. $$

Then there exist real coefficients $b^{(1)}_{0},b^{(1)}_{1},\dots,b_{s}^{(1)}$ , with $b_{0}^{(1)}=\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}\omega_{0}$ , such that

$$ \displaystyle f^{\ast}(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{s}b^{(1)}_{j}h_{j}(x) $$

satisfies $[\mathcal{A}f^{\ast}](x)=g(x)$ for all $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}$ . Moreover, $f^{\ast}$ minimizes $\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f;c)$ over all $f\in\mathcal{F}$ .

#### Lemma B.3.

The minimizer $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ over $\mathcal{F}$ is uniquely determined on $\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}\setminus\{0\}$ .

With these lemmas in hand, we can now prove Theorem 3.1. Substituting the definitions of $\mu_{0},\{\mu_{j}\}_{j}$ into equation (B.3), we obtain

$$ f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{s}b^{(1)}_{j}h_{j}(x)=\frac{\sum_{j=0}^{s}b^{(1)}_{j}\mu_{j}(x)}{w(x)}=\frac{b_{0}^{(1)}\mu_{0}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}b^{(1)}_{j}\mu_{j}(x)}{\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}x+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\,\mu_{0}(x)}. $$

Recall the explicit Radon-Nikodym derivatives $\mu_{0}$ and $\{\mu_{j}\}_{j}$ from Lemma A.14, which share the common denominator $\omega_{0}\nu(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\omega_{i}\nu_{-i}(x)$ . Canceling this common denominator from the numerator and the denominator yields

$$ f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)=\frac{b_{0}^{(1)}\nu(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}b_{j}^{(1)}\nu_{-j}(x)}{\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}x\!\left(\omega_{0}\nu(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\omega_{j}\nu_{-j}(x)\right)+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\nu(x)},\qquad x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}, $$

which is exactly the form stated in Theorem 3.1(b). The only thing left to check is that $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}\in\mathcal{F}$ . Note that $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ has no poles in $\mathcal{S}_{c}$ because $\nu_{j}(x)>0$ for all $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}$ hence $\nu(x),\nu_{-j}(x)>0$ for all $j$ (see A.6.3). On $\mathcal{A}_{c}$ , evaluating at $x=x_{j}^{\star}$ and using Remark A.13 the denominator reduces to $\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}x_{j}^{\star}\cdot\omega_{j}\,\nu_{-j}(x_{j}^{\star})\neq 0$ , since $\omega_{j}\neq 0$ and $\nu_{-j}(x_{j}^{\star})\neq 0$ by Remark A.13. We deduce that the denominator of $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ does not vanish on $\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}$ . Finally, since the Radon-Nikodym derivatives $\nu_{j}(x)$ are affine functions, both numerator and denominator are polynomials in $x$ , hence continuous on a neighborhood of $\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}$ , confirming $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}\in\mathcal{F}$ . This completes the proof of Theorem 3.1(a) and (b). For a proof of Theorem 3.1(c), we refer the reader to Lemma D.1, which proves a more general result.

### B.2 Proof of Lemma B.1

#### Proof.

Using the model $\bm{y}=\bm{X}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}+\bm{\varepsilon}$ , it follows immediately from the definition of $\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{f}$ that

$$ \widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{f}=\bm{W}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{W}^{\top}\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}}{n}=\bm{W}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{W}^{\top}\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}}{n}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}+\bm{W}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{W}^{\top}\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}}{n}, $$

or equivalently

$$ \widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{f}=\bm{W}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{\Lambda}\bm{W}^{\top}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}+\bm{W}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{W}^{\top}\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}}{n}. $$

Since $f(\bm{\Lambda})$ and $\bm{\Lambda}$ are diagonal matrices, they commute, and therefore

$$ \displaystyle\widehat{{\bm{\beta}}}_{f}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}=-\bm{W}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bigr)\bm{W}^{\top}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}+\bm{W}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{W}^{\top}\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}}{n}. $$

Expanding the squared $\bm{\Sigma}$ norm as a quadratic gives

$$ \displaystyle\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{f}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2} \displaystyle={\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{W}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bigr)\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{W}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bigr)\bm{W}^{\top}{\bm{\beta}}_{0} \displaystyle\quad-2\,{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{W}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bigr)\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{W}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{W}^{\top}\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}}{n} \displaystyle\quad+\frac{\bm{\varepsilon}^{\top}\bm{X}}{n}\bm{W}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{W}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{W}^{\top}\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}}{n}. $$

Alternatively,

$$ \|\widehat{{\bm{\beta}}}_{f}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}=\mathcal{B}_{f}(\bm{X},\bm{y})+\mathcal{V}_{f}(\bm{X},\bm{y})+\mathcal{E}_{f}(\bm{X},\bm{y}), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{f}(\bm{X},\bm{y}) \displaystyle:={\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{W}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bigr)\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{W}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bigr)\bm{W}^{\top}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}, \displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{f}(\bm{X},\bm{y}) \displaystyle:=\frac{\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}}{n^{2}}{\sf tr}\left(\bm{X}f(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}){\bm{\Sigma}}f(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}})\bm{X}^{\top}\right)=\frac{\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}}{n}{\sf tr}\left(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}f(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}){\bm{\Sigma}}f(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}})\right), \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{f}(\bm{X},\bm{y}) \displaystyle:=-2\,{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{W}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bigr)\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{W}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{W}^{\top}\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}}{n}+\left[\frac{{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{\top}\bm{X}f(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}){\bm{\Sigma}}f(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}})\bm{X}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}}{n^{2}}-\mathcal{V}_{f}(\bm{X},\bm{y})\right]. $$

Using the spike decomposition ${\bm{\Sigma}}=\sigma_{0}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{p}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top},$ and cyclicity of trace, the bias and variance terms become

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{f}(\bm{X},\bm{y}) \displaystyle=\sigma_{0}^{2}\cdot{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{W}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bigr)^{2}\bm{W}^{\top}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\left({\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{W}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bigr)\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j}\right)^{2}, $$

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{f}(\bm{X},\bm{y}) \displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}}{n}{\sf tr}\left(\bm{W}\bm{\Lambda}f^{2}(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{W}^{\top}\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\frac{\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}}{n}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{\Lambda}f^{2}(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j}. $$

We start by computing the limit of the bias term $\mathcal{B}_{f}(\bm{X},\bm{y})$ . Note that we can rewrite equation (B.5) using the empirical measures (A.10) and (A.11) defined in Appendix A.5 as

$$ \mathcal{B}_{f}(\bm{X},\bm{y})=\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}\,\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\int\left(1-xf(x)\right)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\widehat{B}_{n}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}({\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j})^{2}\left(\int\left(1-xf(x)\right)\mathrm{d}\widehat{C}_{n}^{\,j}(x)\right)^{2} $$

for all sufficiently large $n$ , since Assumption 2.5 guarantees that $|f(d_{i})|<\infty$ for all eigenvalues $d_{i}$ of $\widehat{{\bm{\Sigma}}}$ eventually almost surely.

Using Lemma A.7 and Lemma A.8 we know that $\widehat{B}_{n}\xrightarrow{d}F_{\alpha}$ and $\widehat{C}_{n}^{j}\xrightarrow{}F_{\delta_{j}}$ vaguely. Note that since we do not impose that the functions in $\mathcal{F}$ be compactly supported, extra care is needed to justify the convergence using the weak/vague topology, which is elaborated in Lemma A.15. Therefore, we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{f}(\bm{X},\bm{y})\xrightarrow{a.s.}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\int(1-xf(x))^{2}\ \mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x)\ +\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\left(\int(1-xf(x))\ \mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j}}(x)\right)^{2}. $$

Similarly, we can rewrite equation (B.6) using the empirical measure (A.12) as

$$ \mathcal{V}_{f}(\bm{X},\bm{y})=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,{\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}}\,p}{n}\int xf^{2}(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\frac{{\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}}}{n}\int xf^{2}(x)\,\mathrm{d}\widehat{D}_{n}^{\,j}(x) $$

for all sufficiently large $n$ , as in the bias term. Using Lemma A.6 and Lemma A.9, we know that $F_{\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}}\xrightarrow{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}$ and $\widehat{D}_{n}^{j}\xrightarrow{d}F_{\delta_{j}}$ . Using Lemma A.15 again we know that both integrals have finite limit as $n,p\to\infty$ . Note that because of the $n$ in the denominator, all spike terms in the sum converge to 0, hence

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{f}(\bm{X},\bm{y})\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,{\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}}c\int xf^{2}(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}. $$

Finally, we prove that

$$ \mathcal{E}_{f}(\bm{X},\bm{y})\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}0. $$

We show that each term in $\mathcal{E}_{f}(\bm{X},\bm{y})$ converges to zero almost surely. Define

$$ \bm{a}_{n}:=2\bm{X}\bm{W}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{W}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bigr)\bm{W}^{\top}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, $$

so that the cross term equals $-\bm{a}_{n}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}/n$ . Its squared Euclidean norm is

$$ \displaystyle\|\bm{a}_{n}\|_{2}^{2} \displaystyle=4\,{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{W}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bigr)\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{W}f(\bm{\Lambda})\underbrace{\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{W}}_{=\,n\bm{\Lambda}}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{W}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bigr)\bm{W}^{\top}{\bm{\beta}}_{0} \displaystyle=4n\,{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{W}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bigr)\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{W}\bm{\Lambda}f^{2}(\bm{\Lambda})\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{W}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{p}-\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda})\bigr)\bm{W}^{\top}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}. $$

Since

$$ \|\mathbf{I}_{p}-\bm{\Lambda}f(\bm{\Lambda})\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\max_{i\in[p]}|1-d_{i}f(d_{i})|\quad\text{and}\quad\|f(\bm{\Lambda})\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\max_{i\in[p]}|f(d_{i})|, $$

and since $f\in\mathcal{F}$ is continuous on a fixed neighborhood of the bulk $\mathcal{S}_{c}$ and in fixed neighborhoods around the outliers $x_{j}^{\star}$ and around 0 (see Assumption 2.5), it follows that almost surely, for all large $n$ , both quantities are bounded by constants depending only on $f$ . Since $\|\bm{W}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=1$ and $\|\bm{\Sigma}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+\max_{j\in[r]}\delta_{j}$ , we conclude that, almost surely,

$$ \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\|\bm{a}_{n}\|_{2}^{2}}{n}<\infty, $$

and hence Lemma A.16 gives $\bm{a}_{n}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}/n\xrightarrow{a.s.}0$ . Similarly, define

$$ \bm{A}_{n}:=\frac{1}{n}\bm{X}f(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}){\bm{\Sigma}}f(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}})\bm{X}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, $$

so that the bracketed term in $\mathcal{E}_{f,n}$ equals ${\bm{\varepsilon}}^{\top}\bm{A}_{n}{\bm{\varepsilon}}/n-\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}{\sf tr}(\bm{A}_{n})/n$ , since

$$ \frac{\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}}{n}{\sf tr}(\bm{A}_{n})=\frac{\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}}{n}{\sf tr}\left(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}f(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}){\bm{\Sigma}}f(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}})\right)=\mathcal{V}_{f,n}(\bm{X}). $$

Its operator norm satisfies

$$ \|\bm{A}_{n}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\,\|f(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}})\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\,\|{\bm{\Sigma}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}, $$

where we used $\|\bm{X}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}/n=\|\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ . By the same argument as above, $\limsup_{n}\|\bm{A}_{n}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ is bounded by a finite constant almost surely, and hence Lemma A.17 gives

$$ \frac{{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{\top}\bm{X}f(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}){\bm{\Sigma}}f(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}})\bm{X}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}}{n^{2}}-\mathcal{V}_{f}(\bm{X},\bm{y})\xrightarrow{a.s.}0. $$

This completes the proof. ∎

### B.3 Proof of Lemma B.2

#### Proof.

First, we need to see how $\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f;c)$ relates to operator $A$ . Expanding everything in $\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f;c)$ in the formula from Lemma B.1we have:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f;c) \displaystyle=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}-2\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\int x\,f(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x)+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\int x^{2}f(x)^{2}\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}-2\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\int xf(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j}} \displaystyle+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\left(\int xf(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j}}\right)^{2}+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,{\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}}\int xf^{2}(x)\ \,\mathrm{d}F_{\rm MP}(x) \displaystyle=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}+\int\Bigl(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}x^{2}+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}\,x\,\mu_{0}(x)\Bigr)\,f(x)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x) \displaystyle\quad-2\int\Bigl(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}x+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\,\alpha_{j}^{2}\,x\,\mu_{j}(x)\Bigr)\,f(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\left(\int x\,f(x)\mu_{j}(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}\right)^{2}. $$

Using the notations we introduced in equation (B.1) we can rewrite the risk as

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f;c) \displaystyle=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}+\int xw(x)f(x)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x) \displaystyle\qquad-\int 2x\,g(x)w(x)\,f(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\left(\int xw(x)h_{j}(x)f(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x)\right)^{2} \displaystyle=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}+\langle f,f\rangle_{w}-2\,\langle f,\,g\rangle_{w}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\,\langle f,h_{j}\rangle_{w}^{2}, $$

where in the last line we use the $xw(x)$ -weighted inner product, as defined in (B.2). Recall the definition of $A:\mathcal{F}\to\mathcal{F}$

$$ \mathcal{A}f=f+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\langle f,h_{j}\rangle_{w}\,h_{j}. $$

Thus, the function (B.10) we want to minimize is

$$ \|f\|_{w}^{2}-2\langle f,g\rangle_{w}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\,\langle f,h_{j}\rangle_{w}^{2}=\langle\mathcal{A}f,f\rangle_{w}-2\langle f,g\rangle_{w}. $$

Note that $\mathcal{A}$ is self-adjoint with respect to $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{w}$ because

$$ \langle\phi,\mathcal{A}\psi\rangle_{w}=\langle\mathcal{A}\phi,\psi\rangle_{w}=\langle\phi,\psi\rangle_{w}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\langle\phi,h_{j}\rangle_{w}\langle\psi,h_{j}\rangle_{w}, $$

and positive-semidefinite, as

$$ \langle\mathcal{A}\psi,\psi\rangle_{w}=\|\psi\|_{w}^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\langle\psi,h_{j}\rangle_{w}^{2}\geq\|\psi\|_{w}^{2}. $$

First, let us show $f^{\ast}$ exists. Recall from Lemma A.14 that

$$ \omega_{0}\mu_{0}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\omega_{j}\mu_{j}(x)=1, $$

so from Proposition B.1 we can rewrite

$$ \displaystyle g(x) \displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\mu_{j}(x)}{w(x)}=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}(\omega_{0}\mu_{0}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\omega_{j}\mu_{j}(x))+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\mu_{j}(x)}{w(x)} \displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\mu_{0}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}(\delta_{j}+\sigma_{0}^{2})\alpha_{j}^{2}\mu_{j}(x)}{w(x)}=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}h_{0}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}(\delta_{j}+\sigma_{0}^{2})\alpha_{j}^{2}h_{j}(x). $$

We consider a candidate of the form

$$ f^{\ast}(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{s}b^{(1)}_{j}h_{j}(x). $$

We wish to find real coefficients $\{b^{(1)}_{0},b^{(1)}_{1},\dots,b^{(1)}_{s}\}$ for which

$$ \mathcal{A}f^{\ast}=\sum_{i=0}^{s}b^{(1)}_{i}h_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\left(\sum_{i=0}^{s}b^{(1)}_{i}\langle h_{i},h_{j}\rangle_{w}\right)h_{j} $$

is exactly equal to $g(x)$ . Equivalently, let $\bm{H}$ be the (0-indexed) $(s+1)\times(s+1)$ Gram matrix with $H_{ij}=\langle h_{i},h_{j}\rangle_{w}$ , and define

$$ \mathfrak{D}:=\mathrm{diag}\Bigl(0,\delta_{1}\alpha_{1}^{2},\dots,\delta_{s}\alpha_{s}^{2}\Bigr). $$

Thus, by B.12, the equality $[\mathcal{A}f^{\ast}](x)=g(x)$ on $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}$ is equivalent to solving

$$ \displaystyle\left(\mathbf{I}_{s+1}+\mathfrak{D}\bm{H}\right)\begin{pmatrix}b^{(1)}_{0}\\
b^{(1)}_{1}\\
\vdots\\
b^{(1)}_{s}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\\
(\delta_{1}+\sigma_{0}^{2})\alpha_{1}^{2}\\
\vdots\\
(\delta_{s}+\sigma_{0}^{2})\alpha_{s}^{2}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Since $\bm{H}$ is a Gram matrix, it is positive-semidefinite, hence so is $\mathfrak{D}^{1/2}\bm{H}\mathfrak{D}^{1/2}$ and finally matrix

$$ \displaystyle\mathfrak{D}\bm{H}=\mathfrak{D}^{1/2}({\mathfrak{D}}^{1/2}\bm{H}{\mathfrak{D}}^{1/2}){\mathfrak{D}}^{-1/2} $$

has all eigenvalues non-negative. We conclude that $\mathbf{I}_{s+1}+{\mathfrak{D}}\bm{H}$ is invertible, so we can find the coefficients $\{b_{j}^{(1)}\}_{j=0}^{s}$ that satisfy (B.13). Since $\mathfrak{D}$ has 0 on the first row and column, it is straightforward to see that $b_{0}^{(1)}=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}$ . We are now ready to prove that $f_{\ast}$ is the minimizer. The objective can be rewritten as

$$ \langle\mathcal{A}f,f\rangle_{w}-2\langle f,g\rangle_{w}=\langle\mathcal{A}f,f\rangle_{w}-2\langle f,\mathcal{A}f^{\ast}\rangle_{w}=\left\langle\mathcal{A}(f-f^{\ast}),f-f^{\ast}\right\rangle_{w}-\langle\mathcal{A}f^{\ast},f^{\ast}\rangle_{w} $$

where we used the fact that $\mathcal{A}$ is self-adjoint. Since $f^{\ast}$ is fixed and $\mathcal{A}$ is positive-semidefinite, we conclude that the minimizer is $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}=f^{\ast}$ . The proof of Lemma B.2 now follows. ∎

### B.4 Proof of Lemma B.3

To prove uniqueness, first of all observe that for any $\psi\in\mathcal{F}$ , $\|\psi\|_{w}=0$ if and only if $\psi\equiv 0$ on $\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}\setminus\{0\}$ . This essentially follows from the definition of $\|\cdot\|_{w}$ ; note that,

$$ \|\psi\|_{w}^{2}=\int_{\mathcal{S}_{c}}\psi(x)^{2}xw(x)f_{\alpha}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\psi(x_{j}^{\star})^{2}w(x_{j}^{\star})F_{\alpha}(\{x_{j}^{\star}\})\,. $$

Hence, $\|\psi\|_{w}=0$ if and only if both the terms above are 0. Since $w(x)>0$ for all $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}$ and since $\psi$ is continuous on $\mathcal{S}_{c}$ we must have $\psi\equiv 0$ on $\mathcal{S}_{c}$ . Finally, $\psi$ must also vanish at the atoms of $F_{\alpha}$ , i.e. $\psi(x)=0$ for all $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}\setminus\{0\}$ . Recall from equation (B.11) that $\langle\mathcal{A}\psi,\psi\rangle_{w}\geq\|\psi\|_{w}^{2}$ , so $\langle\mathcal{A}\psi,\psi\rangle_{w}=0$ if and only if $\psi(x)=0$ for all $x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}\setminus\{0\}$ . Next, recall from the proof of Lemma B.2, equation (B.15), that

$$ \mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f;c)=\left\langle\mathcal{A}(f-f^{\ast}),f-f^{\ast}\right\rangle_{w}-\langle\mathcal{A}f^{\ast},f^{\ast}\rangle_{w}+C\,. $$

where $C$ is some constant independent of $f$ . Thus, any minimizer $\widetilde{f}$ of $\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f;c)$ should satisfy $\langle\mathcal{A}(\widetilde{f}-f^{\ast}),\widetilde{f}-f^{\ast}\rangle_{w}=0$ . Since $\langle\mathcal{A}\psi,\psi\rangle_{w}\geq\|\psi\|_{w}^{2}$ we must have $\|\widetilde{f}-f^{\ast}\|_{w}^{2}=0$ and hence $\widetilde{f}=f^{\ast}$ for all points in $\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}$ .

## Appendix C Proof of Lemma 3.2 and Lemma 3.3

### C.1 Proof of Lemma 3.2

#### Proof.

Note that in the extreme case $\delta=0$ , the spiked measure $F_{\delta}$ is just the MP law $F_{\mathrm{MP}}$ (which essentially follows from the observation that $m_{\delta}(z)=m(z)$ at $\delta=0$ ). Hence, when $\delta_{1}=\dots=\delta_{s}=0$ , we have $F_{\delta_{1}}=\dots=F_{\delta_{s}}=F_{\mathrm{MP}}$ and consequently $F_{\alpha}=F_{\mathrm{MP}}$ . Thus, in the isotropic case:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f;c) \displaystyle\overset{a.s.}{=}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\int(1-xf(x))^{2}\ \mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}(x)+c\,\sigma_{0}^{2}\,{\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}}\int xf^{2}(x)\ \mathrm{d}F_{\rm MP}(x) \displaystyle=\int\left[\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}(1-xf(x))^{2}+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,{\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}}xf^{2}(x)\right]\ \mathrm{d}F_{\rm MP} \displaystyle=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\int x\left[(r^{2}x+c\,{\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}})f(x)^{2}-2r^{2}f(x)\right]\ \mathrm{d}F_{\rm MP}. $$

Note that the term that depends on $f(x)$ is a convex quadratic uniquely minimized at

$$ f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)=\frac{2r^{2}}{2(r^{2}x+c\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2})}=\frac{1}{x+c\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}/r^{2}}=\frac{1}{x+\lambda^{*}}. $$

Since this is a continuous function on the positive real line, $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}\in\mathcal{F}$ , and therefore is the minimizer of $\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}(f;c)$ . This is precisely the optimal tuning parameter $\lambda^{*}$ obtained in [76, 77]. ∎

### C.2 Proof of Lemma 3.3

#### Proof.

We prove this inductively in $t$ . Note that for $t=0$ the representation follows directly from the definition of the Ridge estimator with the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. Assume the equality holds for $t$ , so that

$$ \widehat{{\bm{\beta}}}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{SD}}=f_{t}(\widehat{{\bm{\Sigma}}})\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}}{n}. $$

Let ( $\lambda_{t+1},\xi_{t+1}$ ) be the new hyperparameters and let $\widehat{f}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\}$ be given by

$$ \widehat{f}(x)=\frac{1}{x+\lambda_{t+1}}, $$

where we use the convention $1/0:=0$ when $x=-\lambda_{t+1}$ , consistent with (2.9). Using the closed-form expression (2.5),

$$ \displaystyle\widehat{{\bm{\beta}}}^{(t+1)} \displaystyle=\left(\widehat{{\bm{\Sigma}}}+\lambda_{t+1}\mathbf{I}_{p}\right)^{\dagger}\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\!\left((1-\xi_{t+1})\bm{y}+\xi_{t+1}\,\bm{X}\widehat{{\bm{\beta}}}^{(t)}\right)}{n} \displaystyle=(1-\xi_{t+1})\left(\widehat{{\bm{\Sigma}}}+\lambda_{t+1}\mathbf{I}_{p}\right)^{\dagger}\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}}{n}+\xi_{t+1}\left(\widehat{{\bm{\Sigma}}}+\lambda_{t+1}\mathbf{I}_{p}\right)^{\dagger}\widehat{{\bm{\Sigma}}}\,\widehat{{\bm{\beta}}}^{(t)} \displaystyle=(1-\xi_{t+1})\,\widehat{{\bm{\beta}}}_{\widehat{f}}\;+\;\xi_{t+1}\,\widehat{{\bm{\beta}}}_{\widetilde{f}}, $$

where we define $\widetilde{f}$ by

$$ \widetilde{f}(x):=\frac{x\,f_{t}(x)}{x+\lambda_{t+1}}, $$

again with the convention $\widetilde{f}(-\lambda_{t+1})=0$ . Recall from the induction hypothesis that

$$ \displaystyle f_{t}(x) \displaystyle=\frac{1-\xi_{t}}{x+\lambda_{t}}+\frac{\xi_{t}(1-\xi_{t-1})\,x}{(x+\lambda_{t})(x+\lambda_{t-1})}+\cdots+\frac{\xi_{t}\xi_{t-1}\cdots\xi_{2}(1-\xi_{1})\,x^{t-1}}{(x+\lambda_{t})(x+\lambda_{t-1})\cdots(x+\lambda_{1})} \displaystyle\quad+\frac{\xi_{t}\xi_{t-1}\cdots\xi_{1}\,x^{t}}{(x+\lambda_{t})(x+\lambda_{t-1})\cdots(x+\lambda_{0})}. $$

Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle(1-\xi_{t+1})\widehat{f}(x)+\xi_{t+1}\widetilde{f}(x) \displaystyle=\frac{1-\xi_{t+1}}{x+\lambda_{t+1}}+\frac{\xi_{t+1}\,x\,f_{t}(x)}{x+\lambda_{t+1}} \displaystyle=\frac{1-\xi_{t+1}}{x+\lambda_{t+1}}+\frac{\xi_{t+1}(1-\xi_{t})\,x}{(x+\lambda_{t+1})(x+\lambda_{t})}+\frac{\xi_{t+1}\xi_{t}(1-\xi_{t-1})\,x^{2}}{(x+\lambda_{t+1})(x+\lambda_{t})(x+\lambda_{t-1})} \displaystyle\quad+\cdots+\frac{\xi_{t+1}\xi_{t}\cdots\xi_{2}(1-\xi_{1})\,x^{t}}{(x+\lambda_{t+1})(x+\lambda_{t})\cdots(x+\lambda_{1})}+\frac{\xi_{t+1}\xi_{t}\cdots\xi_{1}\,x^{t+1}}{(x+\lambda_{t+1})(x+\lambda_{t})\cdots(x+\lambda_{0})} \displaystyle=f_{t+1}(x). $$

Combining (C.1) and (C.2), the induction step is complete. ∎

## Appendix D $s$ -step Self Distillation - Proof of Theorem 3.4(a)

### D.1 Proof of Theorem 3.4(a)

A direct implication of Lemma 3.3 is that any shrinkage function achieved by self-distillation is a rational function. Thus, the first step to prove that $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ is achieved by self-distillation is to prove that it is a rational function, which is established in the following lemma:

#### Lemma D.1.

There exist monic real-coefficient polynomials $P$ and $Q$ with $\deg P=s+1$ and $\deg Q=s$ such that

$$ f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)=\frac{Q(x)}{P(x)} $$

for all $x$ . Moreover, $P$ has $s+1$ distinct nonzero real roots, exactly one of which is negative. Finally, none of the roots of $P$ lies in $\overline{\mathcal{S}_{c}}:=\mathcal{S}_{c}\cup\{0,x_{1}^{\star},\dots,x_{s}^{\star}\}$ .

The first claim in the above Lemma is exactly the statement of Theorem 3.1(c). The next Lemma will be used to represent the ratio $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}=Q/P$ in the form of Lemma 3.3:

#### Lemma D.2.

Let $d\geq 0$ be an integer and let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a real polynomial such that $\deg\mathfrak{g}\leq d$ . Let $\mathfrak{q}$ be the coefficient of $x^{d}$ in $\mathfrak{g}$ (if $\deg\mathfrak{g}<d$ then $\mathfrak{q}=0$ ). In addition, let $M$ be a set of $d+1$ distinct real numbers. Then, there exists an ordering $(\gamma_{0},\dots,\gamma_{d})$ of $M$ and $d+1$ real numbers $t_{0},\dots,t_{d}$ such that

- 1. The following holds for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$

$$ \mathfrak{g}(x)=t_{d}(x-\gamma_{d-1})\cdots(x-\gamma_{0})+t_{d-1}x(x-\gamma_{d-2})\cdots(x-\gamma_{0})+\cdots+t_{0}x^{d}. $$

(D.1)

- 2. For all $j\geq 0$ we have

$$ t_{0}+t_{1}+\dots+t_{j}\neq\mathfrak{q}-1. $$

(D.2)

#### Proof of Theorem 3.4(a).

From Lemma D.1 we know that $\deg P=s+1$ and $P$ has $s+1$ distinct non-zero real roots and $\deg Q=s$ . Next, apply Lemma D.2 for $d=s$ , $\mathfrak{g}=Q$ and $M$ to be the set of real roots of $P$ to exhibit an ordering $(\gamma_{0},\dots,\gamma_{s})$ of the roots of $P$ and $s+1$ real numbers $t_{0},\dots,t_{s}$ such that

$$ Q(x)=t_{s}(x-\gamma_{s-1})\cdots(x-\gamma_{0})+t_{s-1}x(x-\gamma_{s-2})\cdots(x-\gamma_{0})+\cdots+t_{0}x^{s} $$

and equation D.2 holds, where $\mathfrak{q}$ is the coefficient of $x^{s}$ monomial in $Q$ . $Q$ is monic, hence $\mathfrak{q}=1$ . Since the display above holds for all $x$ , the coefficient of $x^{s}$ has to be the same, hence $1=t_{0}+t_{1}+\dots+t_{s}$ . Finally we choose

$$ \lambda_{i}=-\gamma_{i},\qquad\qquad\xi_{i}=\frac{t_{0}+t_{1}+\dots+t_{i-1}}{t_{0}+t_{1}+\dots+t_{i}}, $$

which are well-defined due to equation (D.2). Note that

$$ \xi_{s}\dots\xi_{i+1}(1-\xi_{i})=\frac{t_{0}+t_{1}+\dots+t_{s-1}}{t_{0}+t_{1}+\dots+t_{s}}\times\dots\times\frac{t_{0}+t_{1}+\dots+t_{i}}{t_{0}+t_{1}+\dots+t_{i+1}}\times\frac{t_{i}}{t_{0}+t_{1}+\dots+t_{i}}=t_{i}, $$

since the terms in the product cancel alternatively, and the total sum is 1. Since $P$ is monic, then $P(x)=(x-\gamma_{0})\dots(x-\gamma_{s})$ hence

$$ \displaystyle f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x) \displaystyle=\frac{Q(x)}{(x-\gamma_{0})\cdots(x-\gamma_{s})} \displaystyle=\frac{t_{s}(x-\gamma_{s-1})\cdots(x-\gamma_{0})+t_{s-1}x(x-\gamma_{s-2})\cdots(x-\gamma_{0})+\cdots+t_{0}x^{s}}{(x-\gamma_{0})\cdots(x-\gamma_{s})} \displaystyle=\frac{t_{s}}{x-\gamma_{s}}+\frac{t_{s-1}x}{(x-\gamma_{s})(x-\gamma_{s-1})}+\cdots+\frac{t_{0}x^{s}}{(x-\gamma_{s})(x-\gamma_{s-1})\cdots(x-\gamma_{0})} \displaystyle=\frac{1-\xi_{s}}{x+\lambda_{s}}+\frac{\xi_{s}(1-\xi_{s-1})x}{(x+\lambda_{s})(x+\lambda_{s-1})}+\dots+\frac{\xi_{s}\dots\xi_{1}\,x^{s}}{(x+\lambda s)(x+\lambda_{s-1})\dots(x+\lambda_{0})} \displaystyle=f_{s}(x), $$

as defined in Lemma 3.3. We conclude that the optimal shrinkage function $f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ is achieved by $s$ steps of self-distillation, initialized at a Ridge estimator $\widehat{\bm{\beta}}^{(0)}$ with parameter $\lambda_{0}$ . The proof that the Ridge parameters $(\lambda_{0},\dots,\lambda_{s})$ are strictly distinct, exactly $s$ of the $s+1$ Ridge parameters are negative and $-\lambda_{0},\dots,-\lambda_{s}\notin\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}$ follows by Lemma D.1. ∎

### D.2 Proof of Lemma D.1

#### Proof.

Recall from Lemma B.2 that

$$ f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}\omega_{0}\,\nu(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}b_{j}^{(1)}\nu_{-j}(x)}{\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}x\left(\omega_{0}\nu(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\omega_{j}\nu_{-j}(x)\right)+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\nu(x)},\qquad x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}. $$

Consider the denominator

$$ P^{0}(x):={\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}x\left(\omega_{0}\nu(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\omega_{j}\nu_{-j}(x)\right)+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\nu(x)} $$

and the numerator

$$ Q^{0}(x):=\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}\omega_{0}\,\nu(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}b_{j}^{(1)}\nu_{-j}(x). $$

Recall from Lemma A.11 that $\nu_{j}(x)$ is a linear function

$$ \nu_{j}(x)=\frac{\delta_{j}(x_{j}^{\star}-x)}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(\delta_{j}+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,)}. $$

Thus $\nu(x)$ is a degree $s$ polynomial and $\nu_{-j}(x)$ is a degree $s-1$ polynomial for all $j$ (A.14). Hence $P^{0}$ is an $s+1$ degree polynomial with leading coefficient

$$ \mathfrak{p}:=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}(-1)^{s}\prod_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{j}}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(\delta_{j}+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,)}\neq 0. $$

Similarly, $Q^{0}$ is a degree $s$ polynomial with the same leading coefficient $\mathfrak{p}$ . Thus if we define $P=P^{0}/\mathfrak{p}$ and $Q=Q^{0}/\mathfrak{p}$ then

$$ f_{\ast}^{\mathrm{pred}}=\frac{Q^{0}}{P^{0}}=\frac{Q}{P} $$

and $P,Q$ are both monic polynomials. Finally, we need to prove that $P$ or equivalently $P^{0}$ has $s+1$ distinct, non-zero real roots that are not in $\overline{\mathcal{S}_{c}}$ . Recall from the definition of $\nu_{j}$ that $\nu_{j}(x_{j}^{\star})=0$ and $\nu_{j}(x)<0\iff x>x_{j}^{\star}$ . Recall from Lemma A.12 that $\{x_{1}^{\star},\dots,x^{\star}_{s}\}$ are all distinct and larger than all numbers in $\mathcal{S}_{c}$ . Assume without loss of generality that $x_{1}^{\star}<x_{2}^{\star}<\dots<x_{s}^{\star}$ . Recall from Remark A.13 that $\nu_{-i}(x_{j}^{\star})=0$ for all $i\neq j$ . Thus, by definition of $P^{0}$ we have

$$ P^{0}(x_{i}^{\star})=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}x_{i}^{\star}\omega_{i}\nu_{-i}(x_{i}^{\star}). $$

This means that $P^{0}(x_{i}^{\star})$ has the same sign as $(-1)^{i-1}$ since

$$ \nu_{1}(x_{i}^{\star}),\dots,\nu_{i-1}(x_{i}^{\star})<0<\nu_{i+1}(x_{i}^{\star}),\dots,\nu_{s}(x_{i}^{\star}). $$

Thus, the sequence $P^{0}(x_{1}^{\star}),P^{0}(x_{2}^{\star}),\dots,P^{0}(x_{s}^{\star})$ alternates sign, so by the intermediate value theorem there is a root $\gamma_{i}$ of $P^{0}$ such that $x_{i}^{\star}<\gamma_{i}<x_{i+1}^{\star}$ . This gives us $s-1$ real roots and $\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{s-1}\notin\overline{\mathcal{S}_{c}}$ . Next, note that $\lim_{x\to\infty}P^{0}(x)=(-1)^{s}\infty$ and since $P^{0}(x_{s}^{\star})$ has the sign of $(-1)^{s-1}$ there exists another root $\gamma_{s}>x_{s}^{\star}$ , and thus $\gamma_{s}\notin\overline{\mathcal{S}_{c}}$ . Since $P^{0}$ is a degree $s+1$ polynomial, and we found $s$ real roots, we conclude that $P^{0}$ has indeed $s+1$ real roots. Let the other root be $\gamma_{0}$ such that $P^{0}(x)=\mathfrak{p}(x-\gamma_{0})\dots(x-\gamma_{s})$ . By Vieta’s formulae,

$$ P^{0}(0)=c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\nu(0)=\mathfrak{p}(-1)^{s+1}\prod_{j=0}^{s}\gamma_{j}=-\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\prod_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{j}}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,(\delta_{j}+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,)}\prod_{j=0}^{s}\gamma_{j}. $$

Since $\nu_{j}(0)>0$ for all $j$ , we deduce that all terms in $P^{0}(0)$ are positive, hence $P^{0}(0)>0$ . Since $\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{s}$ are all positive, we deduce that $\gamma_{0}<0$ and hence $\gamma_{0}\notin\overline{\mathcal{S}_{c}}$ . The proof is now complete. ∎

### D.3 Proof of Lemma D.2

#### Proof.

We choose the numbers $\gamma_{k},t_{k}$ inductively over $k\leq d$ such that

$$ \mathfrak{g}(\gamma_{k})=t_{k}\gamma_{k}^{d-k}(\gamma_{k}-\gamma_{k-1})\dots(\gamma_{k}-\gamma_{0})+t_{k-1}\gamma_{k}^{d-k+1}(\gamma_{k}-\gamma_{k-2})\dots(\gamma_{k}-\gamma_{0})+\dots+t_{0}\gamma_{k}^{d} $$

and such that (D.2) is satisfied. The base case $k=-1$ (no pairs chosen) is trivial. Next, assume we have chosen $\gamma_{0},\dots,\gamma_{k}$ and $t_{0},\dots,t_{k}$ for some $-1\leq k\leq d-1$ such that (D.2) and (D.4) are satisfied for all $0\leq j\leq k$ . Consider the following polynomial:

$$ \displaystyle R_{k}(x) \displaystyle:=\mathfrak{g}(x)-\Big[t_{0}x^{d}+t_{1}x^{d-1}(x-\gamma_{0})+\dots+t_{k}x^{d-k}(x-\gamma_{0})\dots(x-\gamma_{k-1})\Big] \displaystyle\hskip 130.0002pt+(t_{0}+\dots+t_{k}-\mathfrak{q}+1)x^{d-k-1}(x-\gamma_{0})\dots(x-\gamma_{k}). $$

where for $k=-1$ the bracket term is empty. Note that the bracket term has degree at most $d$ , and so does the last term. Since $\deg\mathfrak{g}\leq d$ , we deduce that $\deg R_{k}\leq d$ . Moreover, we immediately deduce that the coefficient of $x^{d}$ in $R_{k}$ is

$$ \mathfrak{q}-(t_{0}+\dots+t_{k})+(t_{0}+\dots+t_{k}-\mathfrak{q}+1)=1. $$

This means that $\deg R_{k}=d$ hence $R_{k}$ has at most $d$ real roots. Note that by the base case of induction, equation (D.4) yields that $R_{k}$ vanishes at $\gamma_{0},\dots,\gamma_{k}$ . Since $M$ has $d+1$ elements, we can choose $\gamma_{k+1}\neq 0$ that was not chosen before such that $R_{k}(\gamma_{k+1})\neq 0$ . Finally, let

$$ t_{k+1}=\frac{\mathfrak{g}(\gamma_{k+1})-\Big[t_{k}\gamma_{k+1}^{d-k}(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{k-1})\dots(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{0})+\dots+t_{1}\gamma_{k+1}^{d-1}(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{0})+t_{0}\gamma_{k+1}^{d}\Big]}{\gamma_{k+1}^{d-k-1}(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{k})\dots(\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_{0})}, $$

which is well-defined since the roots $\gamma_{0},\dots,\gamma_{k+1}$ are distinct and non-zero. Multiplying both sides of this equality by the denominator yields equation (D.4) for $\gamma_{k+1}$ . Note that
