$$ \widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{agg}}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}=\underbrace{\frac{1}{K}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}){\bm{\beta}}_{0}}_{\mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{agg}}}+\frac{1}{K}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\frac{\bm{X}_{\ell}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}_{\ell}}{n_{\ell}}. $$

Expanding the squared $\bm{\Sigma}$ -norm as a quadratic gives

$$ \displaystyle\|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{agg}}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2} \displaystyle=\|\mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{agg}}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2} \displaystyle\quad+\frac{2}{K^{2}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{K}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\bm{\Sigma}\,\widetilde{f}_{\ell^{\prime}}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell^{\prime}})\frac{\bm{X}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}_{\ell^{\prime}}}{n_{\ell^{\prime}}} \displaystyle\quad+\frac{1}{K^{2}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\frac{\bm{\varepsilon}_{\ell}^{\top}\bm{X}_{\ell}}{n_{\ell}}\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\bm{\Sigma}\,\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\frac{\bm{X}_{\ell}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}_{\ell}}{n_{\ell}} \displaystyle\quad+\frac{2}{K^{2}}\sum_{\ell<\ell^{\prime}}\frac{\bm{\varepsilon}_{\ell}^{\top}\bm{X}_{\ell}}{n_{\ell}}\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\bm{\Sigma}\,\widetilde{f}_{\ell^{\prime}}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell^{\prime}})\frac{\bm{X}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}_{\ell^{\prime}}}{n_{\ell^{\prime}}}. $$

Adding and subtracting the conditional expectation of the diagonal quadratic terms, we can write

$$ \|\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{agg}}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}=\|\mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{agg}}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}+\mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{agg}}+\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{agg}}, $$

where the variance term is

$$ \mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{agg}}=\frac{\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}}{K^{2}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\frac{1}{n_{\ell}}{\sf tr}\left(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}\,\widetilde{f}_{\ell}^{2}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\,\bm{\Sigma}\right):=\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{agg}}_{\ell} $$

and the error term $\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{agg}}$ collects three negligible contributions:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{agg}} \displaystyle:=\frac{2}{K^{2}}\sum_{\ell,\ell^{\prime}=1}^{K}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\bm{\Sigma}\,\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell^{\prime}})\frac{\bm{X}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}_{\ell^{\prime}}}{n_{\ell}^{\prime}} \displaystyle\quad+\frac{1}{K^{2}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\left[\frac{\bm{\varepsilon}_{\ell}^{\top}\bm{X}_{\ell}}{n_{\ell}}\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\bm{\Sigma}\,\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\frac{\bm{X}_{\ell}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}_{\ell}}{n_{\ell}}-\frac{\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}}{n_{\ell}}{\sf tr}\left(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}\,\widetilde{f}_{\ell}^{2}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\,\bm{\Sigma}\right)\right] \displaystyle\quad+\frac{2}{K^{2}}\sum_{\ell<\ell^{\prime}}\frac{\bm{\varepsilon}_{\ell}^{\top}\bm{X}_{\ell}}{n_{\ell}}\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\bm{\Sigma}\,\widetilde{f}_{\ell^{\prime}}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell^{\prime}})\frac{\bm{X}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}_{\ell^{\prime}}}{n_{\ell^{\prime}}}. $$

The first two contributions to $\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{agg}}$ converge to zero almost surely by the same concentration arguments as in Section B.2: the first linear terms vanish by Lemma A.16, the second quadratic terms vanish by Lemma A.17. Finally, we justify that the cross-client term is negligible too. For fixed $\ell\neq\ell^{\prime}$ , define

$$ \bm{a}_{p}:=\frac{1}{n_{\ell^{\prime}}}\bm{X}_{\ell}\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\bm{\Sigma}\,\widetilde{f}_{\ell^{\prime}}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell^{\prime}})\bm{X}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{\ell^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}}, $$

so that the $(\ell,\ell^{\prime})$ cross-client term equals $\bm{a}_{p}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{\ell}/n_{\ell}$ . By independence across machines, the vector $\bm{a}_{p}$ is independent of ${\bm{\varepsilon}}_{\ell}$ . Using $\bm{X}_{\ell}^{\top}\bm{X}_{\ell}=n_{\ell}\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\|\bm{a}_{p}\|_{2}^{2}}{n_{\ell}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{K^{4}n_{\ell^{\prime}}^{2}}\,{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\top}\bm{X}_{\ell^{\prime}}\widetilde{f}_{\ell^{\prime}}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell^{\prime}})\bm{\Sigma}\,\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\,\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}\,\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\bm{\Sigma}\,\widetilde{f}_{\ell^{\prime}}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell^{\prime}})\bm{X}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{\ell^{\prime}} \displaystyle\leq\frac{\|\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\,\|\bm{\Sigma}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\,\|\widetilde{f}_{\ell^{\prime}}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell^{\prime}})\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\,\|\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{K^{4}}\cdot\frac{\|\bm{X}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{\ell^{\prime}}\|_{2}^{2}}{n_{\ell^{\prime}}^{2}}. $$

The first factor is almost surely bounded for large $p$ by the same operator norm bounds of Section B.2. For the second factor, observe that $\|\bm{X}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{\ell^{\prime}}\|^{2}={\bm{\varepsilon}}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\top}(\bm{X}_{\ell^{\prime}}\bm{X}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\top}){\bm{\varepsilon}}_{\ell^{\prime}}$ is a quadratic form in ${\bm{\varepsilon}}_{\ell^{\prime}}$ , with $\bm{X}_{\ell^{\prime}}$ independent of ${\bm{\varepsilon}}_{\ell^{\prime}}$ . Applying Lemma A.17 directly, we obtain

$$ \frac{{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\top}(\bm{X}_{\ell^{\prime}}\bm{X}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\top}){\bm{\varepsilon}}_{\ell^{\prime}}}{n_{\ell^{\prime}}^{2}}-\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\,\frac{{\sf tr}(\bm{X}_{\ell^{\prime}}\bm{X}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\top})}{n_{\ell^{\prime}}^{2}}\xrightarrow{a.s.}0. $$

Moreover,

$$ \sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\,\frac{{\sf tr}(\bm{X}_{\ell^{\prime}}\bm{X}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\top})}{n_{\ell^{\prime}}^{2}}=\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\,\frac{p}{n_{\ell^{\prime}}}\,\frac{1}{p}{\sf tr}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell^{\prime}})\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}c\int x\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}, $$

by the standard Marchenko–Pastur limit from Lemma A.6(a), applied to client $\ell^{\prime}$ . We therefore deduce that

$$ \lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{\|\bm{X}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{\ell^{\prime}}\|_{2}^{2}}{n_{\ell^{\prime}}^{2}}=\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}c\int x\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}<\infty, $$

hence $\limsup_{p}\|\bm{a}_{p}\|^{2}/n_{\ell}<\infty$ almost surely, and Lemma A.16 gives $\bm{a}_{p}^{\top}{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{\ell}/n_{\ell}\xrightarrow{a.s.}0$ . This concludes the proof. ∎

### I.4 Proof of Lemma I.3

#### Proof.

By definition of the ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ -norm,

$$ \left\|\frac{1}{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}){\bm{\beta}}_{0}\right\|^{2}_{{\bm{\Sigma}}}=\frac{1}{K^{2}}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\right){\bm{\Sigma}}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\right){\bm{\beta}}_{0}. $$

Using the spiked decomposition of the covariance ${\bm{\Sigma}}=\sigma_{0}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{p}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top},$ we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\frac{1}{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}){\bm{\beta}}_{0}\right\|^{2}_{{\bm{\Sigma}}} \displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}}{K^{2}}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\right)^{2}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}+\frac{1}{K^{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\,{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\right)\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\right){\bm{\beta}}_{0}. $$

Now each matrix $g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})$ is symmetric, because it is obtained by applying a spectral shrinkage function to the symmetric matrix $\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}$ . Hence the sum $\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})$ is also symmetric, and so

$$ {\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\right)\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\right){\bm{\beta}}_{0}=\left[{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}g_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\right)\bm{v}_{j}\right]^{2}. $$

which gives exactly the claimed decomposition. ∎

### I.5 Proof of Lemma I.4

#### Proof.

Using the decomposition from Lemma I.2 and Lemma I.3, it is enough to compute the limit of each term $\mathcal{B}_{0}^{\mathrm{agg}},\mathcal{B}_{j}^{\mathrm{agg}},\mathcal{V}_{\ell}^{\mathrm{agg}}$ individually. First, note that for each $\ell\in\{1,2,\dots K\}$

$$ \mathcal{V}_{\ell}^{\mathrm{agg}}\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\frac{c\sigma_{0}^{2}{\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}}}{K^{2}}\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(x)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}(x) $$

follows mutatis mutandis from the result in (B.9). Similarly, for each $j\in\{1,2,\dots,s\}$ ,

$$ K^{2}\mathcal{B}_{j}^{\mathrm{agg}}\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\int(x\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(x)-1)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j}}\right)^{2}, $$

which can be rearranged to

$$ \displaystyle K^{2}\mathcal{B}_{j}^{\mathrm{agg}} \displaystyle\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\int(x\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(x)-1)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j}}\right)^{2}=\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\left[\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j}}\right)^{2}-2K\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j}}+K^{2}\right]. $$

The proof follows by the same method as in (B.7), using the corresponding empirical measure $\widehat{C}_{n}^{j}$ (see Lemma A.8) of each client and adding the limits together. We skip the details for the sake of brevity. Finally, using Theorem 3.10, we can immediately find the contribution of the bulk bias $\mathcal{B}_{0}^{\mathrm{agg}}$ as follows

$$ \frac{K^{2}\mathcal{B}_{0}^{\mathrm{agg}}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}}\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}2\omega_{0}\sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\int g_{\ell}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}\cdot\int g_{\ell^{\prime}}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}+2\sum_{j=1}^{s}\omega_{j}\sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\left(\int g_{\ell}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j}}\right)\left(\int g_{\ell^{\prime}}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j}}\right)+\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\int g_{\ell}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}. $$

Using the definition of $g_{\ell}$ in Lemma I.1 we obtain

$$ \displaystyle K^{2}\mathcal{B}_{0}^{\mathrm{agg}} \displaystyle\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}2\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}\omega_{0}\left[\sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\left(\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}\right)\left(\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell^{\prime}}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}\right)-(K-1)\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}+\binom{K}{2}\right] \displaystyle\quad+2\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{s}\omega_{j}\left[\sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\left(\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j}}\right)\left(\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell^{\prime}}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j}}\right)-(K-1)\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j}}+\binom{K}{2}\right] \displaystyle\quad+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\left[\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\int x^{2}\widetilde{f}_{\ell}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}-2\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}+K\right]. $$

Therefore, using the Radon-Nikodym derivatives from Lemma A.14, and collecting all terms together, the full limit is

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}_{K}(\widetilde{f}_{1},\dots,\widetilde{f}_{K}) \displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\int\left(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}x^{2}+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,{\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}}x\mu_{0}(x)\right)\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(x)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x) \displaystyle\quad-2\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(x)\left[\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}(K-1)\mu_{0}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\alpha_{j}^{2}\left(K\delta_{j}+\sigma_{0}^{2}(K-1)\right)\mu_{j}(x)\right]\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x) \displaystyle\quad+2\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\left(\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\mu_{0}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}\right)\left(\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell^{\prime}}\mu_{0}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}\right) \displaystyle\quad+2\sum_{j=1}^{s}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\alpha_{j}^{2}\sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\left(\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\mu_{j}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}\right)\left(\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell^{\prime}}\mu_{j}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}\right) \displaystyle\quad+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\mu_{j}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}\right)^{2}+K^{2}\left(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\right). $$

Recall now from Lemma A.14 that

$$ \omega_{0}\mu_{0}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\omega_{j}\mu_{j}(x)=1\qquad\text{for all }x\in\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}, $$

and $\alpha_{j}^{2}=r^{2}\omega_{j}$ , so we can simplify the linear term to obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}_{K}(\widetilde{f}_{1},\dots,\widetilde{f}_{K}) \displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\int\left(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}x^{2}+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,{\sigma_{{\bm{\varepsilon}}}^{2}}x\mu_{0}(x)\right)\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(x)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x) \displaystyle\quad-2\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell}(x)\left[\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}K+K\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\mu_{j}(x)\right]\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x) \displaystyle\quad+2\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\left(\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\mu_{0}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}\right)\left(\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell^{\prime}}\mu_{0}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}\right) \displaystyle\quad+2\sum_{j=1}^{s}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\alpha_{j}^{2}\sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\left(\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\mu_{j}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}\right)\left(\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell^{\prime}}\mu_{j}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}\right) \displaystyle\quad+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\int x\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\mu_{j}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}\right)^{2}+K^{2}\left(r^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\right). $$

Using the auxiliary functions defined in (B.1), and the definition of the $xw(x)$ -weighted inner product (B.2) conclusion follows by straightforward algebraic manipulations. ∎

### I.6 Proof of Lemma I.5

#### Proof.

Substituting $\widetilde{f}_{\ell}=\bar{\vartheta}+\vartheta_{\ell}$ , we first compute

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\|\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\|_{w}^{2}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\|\bar{\vartheta}+\vartheta_{\ell}\|_{w}^{2}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\|\vartheta_{\ell}\|_{w}^{2}+2\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\langle\vartheta_{\ell},\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}+K\|\bar{\vartheta}\|_{w}^{2}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\|\vartheta_{\ell}\|_{w}^{2}+K\|\bar{\vartheta}\|_{w}^{2}. $$

where the middle term vanishes since $\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\vartheta_{\ell}=0$ . Next,

$$ \displaystyle-2K\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\langle g,\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\rangle_{w}=-2K\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\langle g,\bar{\vartheta}+\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}=-2K^{2}\langle g,\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}, $$

again because $\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\vartheta_{\ell}=0$ . Now fix $j\in\{0,1,\dots,s\}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\langle h_{j},\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\rangle_{w}\langle h_{j},\widetilde{f}_{\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{w} \displaystyle=\sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\bigl(\langle h_{j},\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}+\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}\bigr)\bigl(\langle h_{j},\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}+\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{w}\bigr) \displaystyle=\binom{K}{2}\langle h_{j},\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}^{2}+\langle h_{j},\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}\sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\bigl(\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}+\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{w}\bigr)+\sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{w}. $$

Because each $\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}$ appears exactly $K-1$ times in the mixed sum,

$$ \sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\bigl(\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}+\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{w}\bigr)=(K-1)\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}=0, $$

and so

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\langle h_{j},\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\rangle_{w}\langle h_{j},\widetilde{f}_{\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{w}=\binom{K}{2}\langle h_{j},\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}^{2}+\sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{w}. $$

Also, it is immediate by definition that

$$ \displaystyle\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\langle h_{j},\widetilde{f}_{\ell}\rangle_{w}\right)^{2}=K^{2}\langle h_{j},\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}^{2}. $$

Collecting the above identities (I.5), (I.6), (I.7) and (I.8) gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}_{K}(\widetilde{f}_{1},\dots,\widetilde{f}_{K}) \displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\|\vartheta_{\ell}\|_{w}^{2}K\|\bar{\vartheta}\|_{w}^{2}-2K^{2}\langle g,\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}+2\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\langle h_{0},\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}\langle h_{0},\vartheta_{\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{w} \displaystyle+2\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\binom{K}{2}\langle h_{0},\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}^{2}+2\sum_{j=1}^{s}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\alpha_{j}^{2}\left[\binom{K}{2}\langle h_{j},\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}^{2}+\sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{w}\right] \displaystyle+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}K^{2}\langle h_{j},\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}^{2}+K^{2}\left(r^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\right). $$

Finally, since $\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}=0$ , we use

$$ \left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}\right)^{2}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}^{2}+2\sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{w}=0, $$

which implies that

$$ \sum_{\ell<{\ell^{\prime}}}\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{w}=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}^{2}. $$

Substituting this identity for $j=0,1,\dots,s$ yields

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{pred}}_{K}(\widetilde{f}_{1},\dots,\widetilde{f}_{K}) \displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\|\vartheta_{\ell}\|_{w}^{2}-\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\langle h_{0},\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}^{2}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\alpha_{j}^{2}\,\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\langle h_{j},\vartheta_{\ell}\rangle_{w}^{2} \displaystyle+K\|\bar{\vartheta}\|_{w}^{2}-2K^{2}\langle g,\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\,K(K-1)\langle h_{0},\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}^{2} \displaystyle+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\alpha_{j}^{2}\bigl(K(K-1)\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+\delta_{j}K^{2}\bigr)\langle h_{j},\bar{\vartheta}\rangle_{w}^{2}+K^{2}\left(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}\right), $$

which is exactly the claimed formula. ∎

### I.7 Proof of Lemma I.6

#### Proof.

We first rewrite the quadratic terms using the definitions from Lemma A.14 and (B.1). For the bulk term,

$$ \displaystyle\langle h_{0},\phi\rangle_{w} \displaystyle=\int x\,\phi(x)\,w(x)\,h_{0}(x)\,dF_{\alpha}(x)=\int x\,\phi(x)\,\mu_{0}(x)\,dF_{\alpha}(x)=\int x\,\phi(x)\,dF_{\mathrm{MP}}(x), $$

and therefore

$$ \sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\langle h_{0},\phi\rangle_{w}^{2}=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\left(\int x\,\phi(x)\,dF_{\mathrm{MP}}(x)\right)^{2}. $$

Similarly, for each spike $j$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\langle h_{j},\phi\rangle_{w} \displaystyle=\int x\,\phi(x)\,w(x)\,h_{j}(x)\,dF_{\alpha}(x)=\int x\,\phi(x)\,\mu_{j}(x)\,dF_{\alpha}(x)=\int x\,\phi(x)\,dF_{\delta_{j}}(x), $$

so that

$$ \alpha_{j}^{2}\langle h_{j},\phi\rangle_{w}^{2}=\alpha_{j}^{2}\left(\int x\,\phi(x)\,dF_{\delta_{j}}(x)\right)^{2}. $$

Next, since $\mu_{0}(x)\geq 0$ on $\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\|\phi\|_{w}^{2} \displaystyle=\int x\,\phi(x)^{2}\,w(x)\,dF_{\alpha}(x) \displaystyle=\int x\,\phi(x)^{2}\bigl(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}x+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\mu_{0}(x)\bigr)\,dF_{\alpha}(x) \displaystyle\geq\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\int x^{2}\phi(x)^{2}\,dF_{\alpha}(x). $$

Recall from Lemma A.7 that $F_{\alpha}$ decomposes as a mixture, hence

$$ \sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\int x^{2}\phi(x)^{2}\,dF_{\alpha}(x)=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\int x^{2}\phi(x)^{2}\,dF_{\mathrm{MP}}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\alpha_{j}^{2}\,\int x^{2}\phi(x)^{2}\,dF_{\delta_{j}}(x), $$

where we used $\alpha_{j}^{2}=r^{2}\omega_{j}$ . Applying Cauchy–Schwarz with respect to the probability measures $F_{\mathrm{MP}}$ and $F_{\delta_{j}}$ gives

$$ \left(\int x\,\phi(x)\,dF_{\mathrm{MP}}(x)\right)^{2}\leq\int x^{2}\phi(x)^{2}\,dF_{\mathrm{MP}}(x), $$

and, for each $j$ ,

$$ \left(\int x\,\phi(x)\,dF_{\delta_{j}}(x)\right)^{2}\leq\int x^{2}\phi(x)^{2}\,dF_{\delta_{j}}(x). $$

Combining the previous displays, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\langle h_{0},\phi\rangle_{w}^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\alpha_{j}^{2}\,\langle h_{j},\phi\rangle_{w}^{2} \displaystyle\leq\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\int x^{2}\phi(x)^{2}\,dF_{\mathrm{MP}}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\alpha_{j}^{2}\,\int x^{2}\phi(x)^{2}\,dF_{\delta_{j}}(x) \displaystyle=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\int x^{2}\phi(x)^{2}\,dF_{\alpha}(x) \displaystyle\leq\|\phi\|_{w}^{2}. $$

This proves the inequality. For equality to hold, equality must occur in every step above. In particular,

$$ \int x\,\phi(x)^{2}\,\mu_{0}(x)\,dF_{\alpha}(x)=0. $$

Since the integrand is nonnegative and $\mu_{0}(x)>0$ on $\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}$ , this implies $\phi(x)=0$ on $\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}$ . Conversely, if $\phi$ vanishes on $\mathcal{S}_{c}^{+}$ , then every term above is equal to zero, so equality holds. ∎

### I.8 Analysis of Assumption 3.8

Recall from equation (I.2) that $b^{(K)}_{0}$ is found by solving the following linear system:

$$ \displaystyle\left(\mathbf{I}_{s+1}+\mathfrak{D}_{K}\bm{H}\right)\begin{pmatrix}b^{(K)}_{0}\\
b^{(K)}_{1}\\
\vdots\\
b^{(K)}_{s}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\\
(\delta_{1}+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,)\alpha_{1}^{2}\\
\vdots\\
(\delta_{s}+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,)\alpha_{s}^{2}\end{pmatrix}. $$

In this section, we present certain conditions under which $b^{(K)}_{0}\neq 0$ , and further strengthen this property with simulations.

#### I.8.1 Isotropic Model

We begin with the isotropic case ${\bm{\Sigma}}=\sigma_{0}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{p}$ , corresponding to $s=0$ , in which the system (I.2) can be solved explicitly.

#### Proposition I.7.

Assume $s=0$ . Then for every integer $K\geq 1$ , the coefficient $b^{(K)}_{0}$ from (I.2) is given by

$$ b^{(K)}_{0}=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}}{1+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}(K-1)\langle h_{0},h_{0}\rangle_{w}}, $$

and in particular $b^{(K)}_{0}>0$ .

#### Proof.

If $s=0$ , then $\omega_{0}=1$ since we have no spike directions and the system reduces to the scalar equation

$$ \left(1+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}(K-1)\|h_{0}\|_{w}^{2}\right)b^{(K)}_{0}=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}. $$

Hence

$$ b^{(K)}_{0}=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}}{1+\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}(K-1)\|h_{0}\|_{w}^{2}}. $$

Since $\|h_{0}\|_{w}^{2}\geq 0$ , the denominator is strictly positive, so $b^{(K)}_{0}>0$ . ∎

Using equation (I.4), we deduce that

$$ \rho_{\ast,1}=\cdots=\rho_{\ast,K}=\frac{b^{(K)}_{0}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}}=\frac{1}{1+\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}(K-1)\|h_{0}\|_{w}^{2}}, $$

and

$$ f^{\rm pred}_{*,1}=\cdots=f^{\rm pred}_{*,K}=f_{K}^{\ast}\,, $$

where

$$ f_{K}^{\ast}(x)=\frac{b^{(K)}_{0}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}x+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}}=\frac{b^{(K)}_{0}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{x+c\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}/r^{2}}. $$

Thus, the optimal shrinkage rule for each client corresponds to tuned Ridge and for $\sigma_{0}^{2}=1$ we recover the aggregated estimator from Theorem 4.5 in [86].

#### I.8.2 One-Spike Model

In this section, we analyze the one-spike case, ${\bm{\Sigma}}=\sigma_{0}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{p}+\delta_{1}\bm{v}_{1}\bm{v}_{1}^{\top}$ . To simplify the notation, we write

$$ \delta:=\delta_{1},\qquad\omega:=\omega_{1},\qquad\omega_{0}=1-\omega,\qquad\alpha^{2}=r^{2}\omega. $$

#### Proposition I.8.

Assume $s=1$ . Then for every integer $K\geq 1$ , the coefficient $b^{(K)}_{0}$ from (I.2) satisfies $b^{(K)}_{0}>0$ . In particular, $b^{(K)}_{0}\neq 0$ .

#### Proof.

When $s=1$ , the linear system I.2 becomes

$$ \begin{pmatrix}1+(K-1)\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\langle h_{0},h_{0}\rangle_{w}&(K-1)\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\langle h_{0},h_{1}\rangle_{w}\\[2.84526pt]
\bigl((K-1)\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+K\delta\bigr)\alpha^{2}\langle h_{1},h_{0}\rangle_{w}&1+\bigl((K-1)\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+K\delta\bigr)\alpha^{2}\langle h_{1},h_{1}\rangle_{w}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}b^{(K)}_{0}\\
b^{(K)}_{1}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}\\
(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+\delta)\alpha^{2}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Since $\langle h_{1},h_{0}\rangle_{w}=\langle h_{0},h_{1}\rangle_{w}$ , Cramer’s rule gives

$$ \displaystyle b^{(K)}_{0} \displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}\omega_{0}\Bigl(1+\bigl((K-1)\sigma_{0}^{2}+K\delta\bigr)\alpha^{2}\langle h_{1},h_{1}\rangle_{w}\Bigr)-(K-1)\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}\omega_{0}(\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta)\alpha^{2}\langle h_{0},h_{1}\rangle_{w}}{{\sf det}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{2}+\mathfrak{D}_{K}\bm{H}\bigr)} \displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}\omega_{0}\Bigl[1+\delta\alpha^{2}\langle h_{1},h_{1}\rangle_{w}+(K-1)(\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta)\alpha^{2}\bigl(\langle h_{1},h_{1}\rangle_{w}-\langle h_{0},h_{1}\rangle_{w}\bigr)\Bigr]}{{\sf det}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{2}+\mathfrak{D}_{K}\bm{H}\bigr)}. $$

By the same argument as in B.14, the denominator is positive, thus it is enough to prove that

$$ \langle h_{1},h_{1}\rangle_{w}-\langle h_{0},h_{1}\rangle_{w}\geq 0, $$

or equivalently, using equation B.1

$$ \langle h_{1},h_{1}\rangle_{w}-\langle h_{0},h_{1}\rangle_{w}=\int xw(x)h_{1}(x)(h_{1}(x)-h_{0}(x))\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}=\int x(h_{1}(x)-h_{0}(x))\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta}\geq 0. $$

Specializing the formulas in Lemma A.14 to $s=1$ we have

$$ \mu_{0}(x)=\frac{\nu(x)}{(1-\omega)\nu(x)+\omega},\qquad\mu_{1}(x)=\frac{1}{\omega_{0}\nu(x)+\omega_{1}},\qquad\nu(x)=\frac{\delta(x_{\delta}^{\star}-x)}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})}, $$

so

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{1}(x)-\mu_{0}(x) \displaystyle=\frac{1-\nu(x)}{(1-\omega)\nu(x)+\omega}\qquad\text{and}\qquad r^{2}x+c\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\mu_{0}(x)=\frac{r^{2}x\bigl[(1-\omega)\nu(x)+\omega\bigr]+c\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\nu(x)}{(1-\omega)\nu(x)+\omega}. $$

Dividing cancels the common denominator:

$$ \displaystyle x(h_{1}-h_{0})=\frac{x(\mu_{1}-\mu_{0})}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}x+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\mu_{0}}=\frac{x(1-\nu(x))}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}x\bigl[(1-\omega)\nu(x)+\omega\bigr]+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\nu(x)}. $$

Using the definition of $x_{\delta}^{\star}$ (see Lemma A.6), we have $x_{\delta}^{\star}=(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})(1+c\sigma_{0}^{2}/\delta)$ , so

$$ c\sigma_{0}^{2}(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})-\delta x_{\delta}^{\star}=c\sigma_{0}^{2}(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})-\delta(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})(1+c\sigma_{0}^{2}/\delta)=-\delta(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2}), $$

and thus

$$ 1-\nu(x)=1-\frac{\delta(x_{\delta}^{\star}-x)}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})}=\frac{c\sigma_{0}^{2}(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})-\delta x_{\delta}^{\star}+\delta x}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})}=\frac{\delta\bigl(x-(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})\bigr)}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})}. $$

Substituting the previous display back in equation (I.10):

$$ \displaystyle\frac{x(\mu_{1}-\mu_{0})}{r^{2}x+c\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\mu_{0}}=\frac{\delta x}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})}\cdot\frac{x-(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})}{r^{2}x\bigl[(1-\omega)\nu(x)+\omega\bigr]+c\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\nu(x)}=\bigl[x-(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})\bigr]\,\phi(x), $$

where

$$ \phi(x)=\frac{\delta x}{\delta(x_{\delta}^{\star}-x)\bigl[(r^{2}-\alpha^{2})x+c\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\bigr]+\alpha^{2}c\sigma_{0}^{2}(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})x}. $$

A quick computation gives

$$ \phi^{\prime}(x)=\frac{\delta^{2}\bigl[(r^{2}-\alpha^{2})x^{2}+c\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}x_{\delta}^{\star}\bigr]}{\left[\delta(x_{\delta}^{\star}-x)\bigl[(r^{2}-\alpha^{2})x+c\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\bigr]+\alpha^{2}c\sigma_{0}^{2}(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})x\right]^{2}}>0, $$

hence $\phi$ is strictly increasing on the support of $F_{\delta}$ . Finally, note that

$$ 1=\int 1\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}=\int\nu(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta}(x)=\frac{\delta}{c\sigma_{0}^{2}(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})}\int\bigl(x_{\delta}^{\star}-x\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta}(x), $$

where in the last step we substituted the definition of $\nu(x)$ . Rearranging gives

$$ \displaystyle\int x\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta}=x_{\delta}^{\star}-\frac{c\sigma_{0}^{2}(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})}{\delta}=(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})\Bigl(1+\frac{c\sigma_{0}^{2}}{\delta}\Bigr)-\frac{c\sigma_{0}^{2}(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})}{\delta}=\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2}, $$

where we used $x_{\delta}^{\star}=(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})(1+c\sigma_{0}^{2}/\delta)$ . Plugging (I.11) into (I.10), we deduce that

$$ \langle h_{1},h_{1}\rangle_{w}-\langle h_{0},h_{1}\rangle_{w}=\int\bigl[x-(\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2})\bigr]\,\phi(x)\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta}. $$

Now let $T$ be a random variable with distribution $F_{\delta}$ . By (I.12), $\mathbb{E}[T]=\delta+\sigma_{0}^{2}$ , so we deduce that

$$ \langle h_{1},h_{1}\rangle_{w}-\langle h_{0},h_{1}\rangle_{w}={\sf cov}(T,\,\phi(T)). $$

Since $\phi$ is strictly increasing on the support of $F_{\delta}$ , the conclusion follows by Chebyshev’s correlation inequality. ∎

#### I.8.3 General case

Finally, for arbitrary number of spikes $s\geq 2$ , we show that only finitely many values of $\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}$ can make $b^{(K)}_{0}$ vanish. We prove this in the next Lemma.

#### Lemma I.9.

Fix $K\geq 2$ , $c>0$ , $r>0$ , $(\delta_{j})_{j=1}^{s}$ , and $(\omega_{j})_{j=0}^{s}$ satisfying Assumption 2.3. Then there exist at most finitely many values of $\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\geq 0$ such that

$$ b^{(K)}_{0}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})=0. $$

#### Proof.

Recall from (I.2) that the vector

$$ b(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}):=\begin{pmatrix}b^{(K)}_{0}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}),&\!\!\!b^{(K)}_{1}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}),&\!\!\!\dots&\!\!\!b^{(K)}_{s}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})\end{pmatrix}\!^{\top} $$

is defined by

$$ \Bigl(\mathbf{I}_{s+1}+\mathfrak{D}_{K}\bm{H}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})\Bigr)b(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}\omega_{0}\\
(\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta_{1})\alpha_{1}^{2}\\
\vdots\\
(\sigma_{0}^{2}+\delta_{s})\alpha_{s}^{2}\end{pmatrix}:=\gamma. $$

We first show that each entry $\bm{H}_{ij}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})$ is real-analytic on $[0,\infty)$ . Since the integrand contains the prefactor $x$ , the atom at $0$ does not contribute. Thus, using the definitions in (B.1),

$$ \bm{H}_{ij}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})=\int_{a}^{b}\frac{x\,\mu_{i}(x)\mu_{j}(x)}{\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}x+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\mu_{0}(x)}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x)+\sum_{\ell=1}^{s}\frac{x_{\ell}^{\star}\,\mu_{i}(x_{\ell}^{\star})\mu_{j}(x_{\ell}^{\star})}{\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}x_{\ell}^{\star}+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\mu_{0}(x_{\ell}^{\star})}\,F_{\alpha}(\{x_{\ell}^{\star}\}). $$

At every nonzero outlier atom $x_{\ell}^{\star}$ , one has

$$ \mu_{0}(x_{\ell}^{\star})=0,\qquad\mu_{i}(x_{j}^{\star})=\omega_{i}^{-1}\mathbf{1}[i=j]. $$

Hence

$$ \displaystyle\bm{H}_{ij}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})=\int_{a}^{b}\frac{x\,\mu_{i}(x)\mu_{j}(x)}{\sigma_{0}^{2}r^{2}x+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\mu_{0}(x)}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x)+\frac{\mathbf{1}[{i=j\geq 1}]}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\alpha_{i}^{2}}\,F_{\alpha}(\{x_{i}^{\star}\}). $$

The outlier term does not depend on $\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}$ . Since $x>0$ on $[a,b]$ ,

$$ r^{2}x+c\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\mu_{0}(x)\geq r^{2}x>0, $$

so the bulk integrand is real-analytic in $\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}$ for every $x\in[a,b]$ . Since $[a,b]$ is compact, differentiation under the integral sign holds on every compact subinterval of $[0,\infty)$ . Hence each $\bm{H}_{ij}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})$ is real-analytic on $[0,\infty)$ , and therefore

$$ b(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})=\Bigl(\mathbf{I}_{s+1}+\mathfrak{D}_{K}\bm{H}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})\Bigr)^{-1}\gamma $$

is real-analytic on $[0,\infty)$ , and in particular so is $b^{(K)}_{0}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})$ . We next prove that

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\to\infty}b^{(K)}_{0}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})=\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}. $$

It suffices to show that $\bm{H}_{0j}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})\to 0$ for all $0\leq j\leq s$ , since then $\bm{H}_{j0}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})\to 0$ by symmetry, and the first row and first column of $\mathbf{I}_{s+1}+\mathfrak{D}_{K}\bm{H}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})$ converge to those of the identity matrix. This implies that the first coordinate of the solution converges to the first coordinate of $\gamma$ , namely $\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}$ . Using (I.13), for all $0\leq j\leq s$ ,

$$ \bm{H}_{0j}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})=\int_{a}^{b}\frac{x\,\mu_{0}(x)\mu_{j}(x)}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}x+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\mu_{0}(x)}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\alpha}(x). $$

For each $x\in[a,b]$ , one has $\mu_{0}(x)>0$ , so

$$ \frac{x\,\mu_{0}(x)\mu_{j}(x)}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}x+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\mu_{0}(x)}\longrightarrow 0\qquad\text{as }\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\to\infty. $$

Moreover,

$$ 0\leq\frac{x\,\mu_{0}(x)\mu_{j}(x)}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}x+c\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\mu_{0}(x)}\leq\frac{x\,\mu_{0}(x)\mu_{j}(x)}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}x}=\frac{\mu_{0}(x)\mu_{j}(x)}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}}, $$

and the right-hand side is integrable on $[a,b]$ . By dominated convergence, $\bm{H}_{0j}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})\to 0$ , and (I.14) follows. In particular, there exists $M>0$ such that $b^{(K)}_{0}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})\neq 0$ for all $\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\geq M$ .

It remains to consider the compact interval $[0,M]$ . Since $b^{(K)}_{0}$ is real-analytic on $[0,M]$ , if it had infinitely many zeros in $[0,M]$ , then by compactness these zeros would have an accumulation point in $[0,M]$ . By the identity theorem for real-analytic functions, $b^{(K)}_{0}$ would then vanish identically on $[0,\infty)$ , contradicting $b^{(K)}_{0}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})\to\sigma_{0}^{2}\,r^{2}\omega_{0}>0$ as $\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\to\infty$ .

Therefore $b^{(K)}_{0}$ has only finitely many zeros in $[0,M]$ and none in $[M,\infty)$ , which proves that there are at most finitely many values of $\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2}\geq 0$ such that $b^{(K)}_{0}(\sigma_{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{2})=0$ . ∎

## Appendix J Quadratic Forms of Products - Proof of Theorem 3.10

In this section, we introduce several technical results needed to prove Theorem 3.10. Recall $m(z)$ and $m_{\delta}(z)$ from Section A.1 and Lemma A.11. Since Theorem 3.10 allows the two matrices to have different aspect ratios $c_{\ell}$ and $c_{k}$ , we use the subscripts $m_{c_{\ell}}(z)$ , $m_{c_{k}}(z)$ and $m_{\delta,\,c_{\ell}}(z)$ , $m_{\delta,\,c_{k}}(z)$ to denote the corresponding Stieltjes transforms throughout this section.

We start by computing limits of products of resolvents of independent covariance matrices in the following preliminary Lemma.

#### Lemma J.1.

Let

$$ \widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}=\frac{\bm{X}_{\ell}^{\top}\bm{X}_{\ell}}{n_{\ell}},\qquad\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k}=\frac{\bm{X}_{k}^{\top}\bm{X}_{k}}{n_{k}} $$

be two independent sample covariance matrices where the rows of $\bm{X}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}\times p}$ and $\bm{X}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}\times p}$ satisfy Assumption 2.1. Assume that $p/n_{\ell}\to c_{\ell}$ and $p/n_{k}\to c_{k}$ . Then, almost surely, for all $z_{\ell},z_{k}\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}^{+}$ we have

$$ \frac{{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}-z_{\ell}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k}-z_{k}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}}{\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\omega_{0}\,m_{c_{\ell}}(z_{\ell})\,m_{c_{k}}(z_{k})+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\omega_{j}\,m_{\delta_{j},\,c_{\ell}}(z_{\ell})\,m_{\delta_{j},\,c_{k}}(z_{k}). $$

For each fixed $z_{\ell},z_{k}$ , almost sure convergence follows from the deterministic equivalents for products of independent random matrices developed in [86, 83]. We then extend this to simultaneous convergence over all $z$ using the following theorem, due to Vitali and Porter; for a proof, see Section 2.4 in [87].

#### Theorem J.2.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ be a connected open set and $\{f_{n}\}$ be a locally bounded sequence of analytic functions on $D$ . If $\lim_{n\to\infty}f_{n}(z)$ exists for each $z$ belonging to a set $E\subseteq D$ which has an accumulation point in $D$ , then $\{f_{n}\}$ converges uniformly on compact subsets of $D$ to an analytic function.

The key argument to prove Theorem 3.10 is that we can extend Lemma J.1 to general functions in $\mathcal{F}$ . The proof of the theorem proceeds in two steps. First, we extend Lemma J.1 from first-order resolvents to arbitrary powers of resolvents. For this first step, we use the following standard Lemma from complex analysis, which is commonly employed in the study of high-dimensional ridge asymptotics; see, for instance, [29, 86, 83]. For a proof, see Lemma 2.14 in [85].

#### Lemma J.3.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ be a connected open set, and let $f_{n}:D\to\mathbb{C}$ be analytic for each $n$ . Assume that the sequence $(f_{n})$ is uniformly bounded on $D$ , that is, there exists $M>0$ such that

$$ |f_{n}(z)|\leq M\qquad\text{for all }n\text{ and all }z\in D. $$

If $f_{n}(z)\to f(z)$ pointwise on $D$ for some analytic function $f$ , then

$$ f_{n}^{\prime}(z)\to f^{\prime}(z)\qquad\text{for all }z\in D. $$

For any analytic function $f$ , we write $f^{(t)}(z)$ for its $t$ -th derivative evaluated at $z$ and for notational convenience, for any analytic function $f$ and any integer $t\geq 1$ , define

$$ f^{[t]}(z):=\frac{1}{(t-1)!}\,f^{(t-1)}(z). $$

Using this notation, we can formalize the following Lemma.

#### Lemma J.4.

Under the Assumptions of Lemma J.1, with probability one, for any integers $t_{\ell},t_{k}\geq 1$ and any $z_{\ell},z_{k}\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}_{+}$ , we have

$$ \frac{{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}-z_{\ell}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-t_{\ell}}(\widehat{\Sigma}_{k}-z_{k}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-t_{k}}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}}{\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\omega_{0}\,m_{c_{\ell}}^{[t_{\ell}]}(z_{\ell})\,m_{c_{k}}^{[t_{k}]}(z_{k})+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\omega_{j}\,m_{\delta_{j},\,c_{\ell}}^{[t_{\ell}]}(z_{\ell})\,m_{\delta_{j},\,c_{k}}^{[t_{k}]}(z_{k}). $$

Fix now any real $\lambda>0$ and let

$$ \phi(x)=a_{0}+\sum_{q=1}^{Q}a_{q}(x+\lambda)^{-q}. $$

By the integral representation of the Stieltjes transform, for every integer $q\geq 1$ ,

$$ m^{[q]}(-\lambda)=\int\frac{1}{(x+\lambda)^{q}}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}}(x),\qquad m_{\delta}^{[q]}(-\lambda)=\int\frac{1}{(x+\lambda)^{q}}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta}(x). $$

Thus

$$ a_{0}+\sum_{q=1}^{Q}a_{q}\,m^{[q]}(-\lambda)=\int\phi\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP}},\qquad a_{0}+\sum_{q=1}^{Q}a_{q}\,m_{\delta}^{[q]}(-\lambda)=\int\phi\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta}. $$

Therefore, since $-\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}^{+}$ , by linearity of the quadratic form and Lemma J.4, we obtain the following extension.

#### Corollary J.5.

Let

$$ \phi(x)=a_{0}+\sum_{q=1}^{Q}a_{q}(x+\lambda_{\ell})^{-q},\qquad\psi(x)=b_{0}+\sum_{t=1}^{T}b_{t}(x+\lambda_{k})^{-t_{k}}, $$

with $\lambda_{\ell},\lambda_{k}>0$ and $a_{0},a_{q},b_{0},b_{t}\in\mathbb{R}$ . Then, with probability one,

$$ \frac{{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\phi(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\psi(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k}){\bm{\beta}}_{0}}{\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\omega_{0}\left(\int\phi\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP},\,c_{\ell}}\right)\left(\int\psi\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP},\,c_{k}}\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\omega_{j}\left(\int\phi\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j},\,c_{\ell}}\right)\left(\int\psi\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j},\,c_{k}}\right). $$

Finally, we can combine Corollary J.5 with the Weierstrass approximation theorem to obtain Theorem 3.10.

#### Proof of Theorem 3.10.

Let $\mathrm{spec}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})$ and $\mathrm{spec}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k})$ be the spectra of $\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}$ and $\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k}$ , respectively. By [68], there exists a deterministic constant $M<\infty$ such that, almost surely, there exists a random $N:=N(\omega)$ such that for $p\geq N$

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{spec}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\cup\mathrm{spec}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k})\subset[0,M]. $$

Next, fix $\phi\in\mathcal{F}_{c_{\ell}}$ and $\psi\in\mathcal{F}_{c_{k}}$ . Since the test functions are only required to be continuous on $\mathcal{S}_{c_{\ell}}$ (resp. $\mathcal{S}_{c_{k}}$ ) and to take finite values at the outliers, we may argue exactly as in Lemma A.15. We first replace $\phi$ and $\psi$ by continuous functions on $[0,M]$ that agree with the originals on $\mathcal{S}_{c_{\ell}}^{+}$ (resp. $\mathcal{S}_{c_{k}}^{+}$ ) and on sufficiently small neighborhoods of the outlier locations. For simplicity, we keep writing $\phi$ and $\psi$ for these extensions. This modification does not affect the argument, since for all large $p$ the eigenvalues of $\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}$ and $\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k}$ lie in the region where the original and extended functions coincide, and the limiting integrals are unchanged for the same reason; see Lemma A.15 for a fully worked-out proof of a similar argument. Now define

$$ \widetilde{\phi}(y):=\phi\left(\frac{1}{y}-1\right),\qquad\widetilde{\psi}(y):=\psi\left(\frac{1}{y}-1\right),\qquad y\in\Bigl[\frac{1}{M+1},1\Bigr]. $$

Since $y\mapsto\frac{1}{y}-1$ is continuous on $\bigl[\frac{1}{M+1},1\bigr]$ , both $\widetilde{\phi}$ and $\widetilde{\psi}$ are continuous on that interval. By the Weierstrass approximation theorem, there exist polynomials $P_{m}$ and $Q_{m}$ such that

$$ \sup_{y\in[\frac{1}{M+1},1]}|P_{m}(y)-\widetilde{\phi}(y)|\xrightarrow{m\to\infty}0,\qquad\sup_{y\in[\frac{1}{M+1},1]}|Q_{m}(y)-\widetilde{\psi}(y)|\xrightarrow{m\to\infty}0. $$

Set

$$ \phi_{m}(x):=P_{m}\left(\frac{1}{x+1}\right),\qquad\psi_{m}(x):=Q_{m}\left(\frac{1}{x+1}\right). $$

Then $\phi_{m},\psi_{m}$ are rational functions as in Corollary J.5, and

$$ \sup_{x\in[0,M]}|\phi_{m}(x)-\phi(x)|\xrightarrow{m\to\infty}0,\qquad\sup_{x\in[0,M]}|\psi_{m}(x)-\psi(x)|\xrightarrow{m\to\infty}0. $$

For $m\geq 1$ , define

$$ L_{p}:=\frac{{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\phi(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\psi(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k}){\bm{\beta}}_{0}}{\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}},\qquad L_{p,m}:=\frac{{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\phi_{m}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\psi_{m}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k}){\bm{\beta}}_{0}}{\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}}, $$

and

$$ R:=\omega_{0}\left(\int\phi\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP},\,c_{\ell}}\right)\left(\int\psi\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP},\,c_{k}}\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\omega_{j}\left(\int\phi\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j},\,c_{\ell}}\right)\left(\int\psi\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j},\,c_{k}}\right), $$

$$ R_{m}:=\omega_{0}\left(\int\phi_{m}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP},\,c_{\ell}}\right)\left(\int\psi_{m}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\mathrm{MP},\,c_{k}}\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\omega_{j}\left(\int\phi_{m}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j},\,c_{\ell}}\right)\left(\int\psi_{m}\,\mathrm{d}F_{\delta_{j},\,c_{k}}\right). $$

For each fixed $m$ , we already know from Corollary J.5 that as $p\to\infty$

$$ \displaystyle L_{p,m}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}R_{m}. $$

Moreover, since $\phi_{m}\xrightarrow{m\to\infty}\phi$ and $\psi_{m}\xrightarrow{m\to\infty}\psi$ uniformly on $[0,M]$ , we deduce that for all probability measures $F\in\{F_{\mathrm{MP}},F_{\delta_{1}},\dots,F_{\delta_{s}}\}$ whose supports are subsets of $[0,M]$ ,

$$ \left|\int\phi_{m}\,\mathrm{d}F-\int\phi\,\mathrm{d}F\right|\leq\sup_{x\in[0,M]}|\phi_{m}(x)-\phi(x)|,\qquad\left|\int\psi_{m}\,\mathrm{d}F-\int\psi\,\mathrm{d}F\right|\leq\sup_{x\in[0,M]}|\psi_{m}(x)-\psi(x)|, $$

and therefore $R_{m}\xrightarrow{m\to\infty}R$ . Next, by the triangle inequality and the bound $|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}A{\bm{\beta}}_{0}|/\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}},$

$$ \displaystyle|L_{p}-L_{p,m}| \displaystyle\leq\left\|\phi(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\psi(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k})-\phi_{m}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\psi_{m}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k})\right\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq\|\phi(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})-\phi_{m}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\|_{\mathrm{op}}\,\|\psi(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k})\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\phi_{m}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\|_{\mathrm{op}}\,\|\psi(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k})-\psi_{m}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k})\|_{\mathrm{op}}. $$

By linearity, for all $p\geq N$ so that (J.1) holds,

$$ \|\phi(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})-\phi_{m}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\sup_{x\in[0,M]}|\phi_{m}(x)-\phi(x)|,\qquad\|\psi(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k})-\psi_{m}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k})\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\sup_{x\in[0,M]}|\psi_{m}(x)-\psi(x)|, $$

and also

$$ \|\psi(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k})\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\sup_{x\in[0,M]}|\psi(x)|,\qquad\|\phi_{m}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell})\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\sup_{x\in[0,M]}|\phi_{m}(x)|. $$

Since $\phi_{m}\to\phi$ uniformly on $[0,M]$ , the quantity $\sup_{x\in[0,M]}|\phi_{m}(x)|$ is bounded by a finite constant. Hence

$$ \sup_{p\geq N}|L_{p}-L_{p,m}|\xrightarrow{m\to\infty}0. $$

Finally, for all $p\geq N$

$$ \displaystyle|L_{p}-R| \displaystyle\leq|L_{p}-L_{p,m}|+|L_{p,m}-R_{m}|+|R_{m}-R| \displaystyle\leq\sup_{p\geq N}|L_{p}-L_{p,m}|+|L_{p,m}-R_{m}|+|R_{m}-R| $$

To conclude fix $\eta>0$ , and choose $m$ large enough such that both the first term and the third term are less than $\eta/3$ . Finally, we can choose $p\geq N$ large enough in such that the middle term is also less than $\eta/3$ by (J.2). The conclusion follows. ∎

### J.1 Proof of Lemma J.1

#### Proof.

First, we prove that for any $z_{\ell},z_{k}\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}^{+}$ conclusion holds almost surely. Recall from (A.4) that, for each $\ell$ , there exists an analytic function $a_{n_{\ell}}(z)$ on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}_{+}$ such that

$$ (\widehat{{\bm{\Sigma}}}_{\ell}-z\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}\asymp(a_{n_{\ell}}(z){\bm{\Sigma}}-z\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1},\qquad z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}_{+}. $$

Similarly for $k$ , there exists an analytic function $a_{n_{k}}(z)$ such that

$$ (\widehat{{\bm{\Sigma}}}_{k}-z\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}\asymp(a_{n_{k}}(z){\bm{\Sigma}}-z\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1},\qquad z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}_{+}. $$

For any $\delta>0$ , define

$$ \displaystyle D_{\delta}:=\{z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}_{+}:\ |\Im z|>\delta\}\cup\{z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}_{+}:\ \Re z<-\delta\}. $$

Since $z_{\ell}$ and $z_{k}$ are fixed and lie outside $\mathbb{R}_{+}$ , there exists $\delta>0$ such that $z_{\ell},z_{k}\in D_{\delta}$ . By the proof of Theorem 3.1(b) in [86] (where $x_{p}(z)$ corresponds to $a_{n_{\ell}}(z)$ or $a_{n_{k}}(z)$ )

$$ \displaystyle\|(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}-z_{\ell}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}\|_{2}\leq\delta^{-1},\qquad\|(a_{n_{\ell}}(z_{\ell}){\bm{\Sigma}}-z_{\ell}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}\|_{2}\leq\delta^{-1}, $$

and similarly for $k$ . Hence the hypotheses of Lemma D.8.4 in [83] are satisfied, and therefore

$$ (\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}-z_{\ell}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k}-z_{k}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}\asymp(a_{n_{\ell}}(z_{\ell}){\bm{\Sigma}}-z_{\ell}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}(a_{n_{k}}(z_{k}){\bm{\Sigma}}-z_{k}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}. $$

In particular, if we let $\bm{\Theta}_{n}={\bm{\beta}}_{0}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}$ in equation (A.4) as in a previous section A.5.1 then

$$ \displaystyle{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}-z_{\ell}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k}-z_{k}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}-{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}(a_{n_{\ell}}{\bm{\Sigma}}-z_{\ell}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}(a_{n_{k}}{\bm{\Sigma}}-z_{k}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}0. $$

so it is enough to compute the limit of the deterministic quadratic form. Recall from Proposition A.5 that

$$ (a_{n_{\ell}}{\bm{\Sigma}}-z_{\ell}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}=\frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n_{\ell}}-z_{\ell}}\left[\mathbf{I}_{p}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\frac{\delta_{j}\,a_{n_{\ell}}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n_{\ell}}-z_{\ell}+\delta_{j}\,a_{n_{\ell}}}\,\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\right], $$

with a similar formula for $k$ . Expanding the product, and using the orthonormality of the spike vectors $v_{1},\dots,v_{s}$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle(a_{n_{\ell}}{\bm{\Sigma}}-z_{\ell}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}(a_{n_{k}}{\bm{\Sigma}}-z_{k}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n_{\ell}}-z_{\ell})(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n_{k}}-z_{k})}\left[\mathbf{I}_{p}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\left(-\frac{\delta_{j}\,a_{n_{\ell}}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n_{\ell}}-z_{\ell}+\delta_{j}\,a_{n_{\ell}}}-\frac{\delta_{j}\,a_{n_{k}}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n_{k}}-z_{k}+\delta_{j}\,a_{n_{k}}}\right.\right. \displaystyle\hskip 136.5733pt\left.\left.+\frac{\delta_{j}\,a_{n_{\ell}}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n_{\ell}}-z_{\ell}+\delta_{j}\,a_{n_{\ell}}}\cdot\frac{\delta_{j}\,a_{n_{k}}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n_{k}}-z_{k}+\delta_{j}\,a_{n_{k}}}\right)\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\right] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n_{\ell}}-z_{\ell})(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n_{k}}-z_{k})}\mathbf{I}_{p}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\left[\frac{1}{(a_{n_{\ell}}(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+\delta_{j})-z_{\ell})(a_{n_{k}}(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+\delta_{j})-z_{k})}-\frac{1}{(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n_{\ell}}-z_{\ell})(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n_{k}}-z_{k})}\right]\bm{v}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}. $$

Taking the quadratic form against ${\bm{\beta}}_{0}$ , we get

$$ \displaystyle{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}(a_{n_{\ell}}{\bm{\Sigma}}-z_{\ell}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}(a_{n_{k}}{\bm{\Sigma}}-z_{k}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}{\bm{\beta}}_{0} \displaystyle=\frac{\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}}{(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n_{\ell}}-z_{\ell})(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n_{k}}-z_{k})}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}({\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j})^{2}\left[\frac{1}{(a_{n_{\ell}}(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+\delta_{j})-z_{\ell})(a_{n_{k}}(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+\delta_{j})-z_{k})}-\frac{1}{(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n_{\ell}}-z_{\ell})(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n_{k}}-z_{k})}\right]. $$

Rearranging terms,

$$ \displaystyle{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}(a_{n_{\ell}}{\bm{\Sigma}}-z_{\ell}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}(a_{n_{k}}{\bm{\Sigma}}-z_{k}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}{\bm{\beta}}_{0} \displaystyle=\left(\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}({\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j})^{2}\right)\frac{1}{(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n_{\ell}}-z_{\ell})(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n_{k}}-z_{k})}+\sum_{j=1}^{s}({\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j})^{2}\frac{1}{(a_{n_{\ell}}(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+\delta_{j})-z_{\ell})(a_{n_{k}}(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+\delta_{j})-z_{k})}. $$

We now let $n\to\infty$ . By Lemma A.4 and equation A.9, we know that

$$ \frac{1}{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,a_{n_{\ell}}-z_{\ell}}\to m_{c_{\ell}}(z_{\ell}),\qquad\frac{1}{a_{n_{\ell}}(\sigma_{0}^{2}\,+\delta_{j})-z_{\ell}}\to m_{\delta_{j},\,c_{\ell}}(z_{\ell}), $$

and similar limits hold for $k$ . Hence

$$ \displaystyle{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}(a_{n_{\ell}}{\bm{\Sigma}}-z_{\ell}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}(a_{n_{k}}{\bm{\Sigma}}-z_{k}\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\left(r^{2}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\alpha_{j}^{2}\right)m_{c_{\ell}}(z_{\ell})m_{c_{k}}(z_{k})+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\alpha_{j}^{2}\,m_{\delta_{j},\,c_{\ell}}(z_{\ell})m_{\delta_{j},\,c_{k}}(z_{k}). $$

The conclusion now follows after dividing by $\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}$ and using equation (J.5).

It remains to promote this to almost sure simultaneous convergence over all $z_{\ell},z_{k}\in D_{\delta}$ on a single probability-one event via a standard density argument. Fix $\delta>0$ , and for all $z,w\in D_{\delta}$ , define

$$ F_{n}(z,w):=\frac{\beta_{0}^{\top}(\widehat{\Sigma}_{\ell}-z\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}(\widehat{\Sigma}_{\ell^{\prime}}-w\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}\beta_{0}}{\|\beta_{0}\|_{2}^{2}},\qquad F(z,w):=\omega_{0}\,m_{c_{\ell}}(z)\,m_{c_{k}}(w)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\omega_{j}\,m_{c_{\ell},\,\delta_{j}}(z)\,m_{c_{k},\,\delta_{j}}(w). $$

Both $F_{n}$ and $F$ are analytic in each variable on $D_{\delta}$ , and by (J.4), $|F_{n}(z,w)|\leq\delta^{-2}$ uniformly in $n$ and $z,w\in D_{\delta}$ . Fix $w\in D_{\delta}$ . By our previous work, $F_{n}(z,w)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}F(z,w)$ for each fixed $z\in D_{\delta}$ . Let $E=\{z_{k}\}_{k\geq 1}\subset D_{\delta}$ be a countable set with an accumulation point in $D_{\delta}$ , and define

$$ \Omega_{0,w}:=\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}\bigl\{\omega:F_{n}(z_{k},w)\to F(z_{k},w)\bigr\}, $$

which satisfies $\mathbb{P}(\Omega_{0,w})=1$ as a countable intersection of almost sure events. On $\Omega_{0,w}$ , the sequence $z\mapsto F_{n}(z,w)$ consists of analytic functions on $D_{\delta}$ , is uniformly bounded by $\delta^{-2}$ , and converges pointwise on $E$ . By Theorem J.2, $F_{n}(\cdot,w)$ converges uniformly on compact subsets of $D_{\delta}$ to an analytic limit. Since this limit agrees with $F(\cdot,w)$ on $E$ , the identity theorem implies that the limit equals $F(\cdot,w)$ on all of $D_{\delta}$ . Hence, on $\Omega_{0,w}$ , $F_{n}(z,w)\to F(z,w)$ for all $z\in D_{\delta}$ . Similarly, we can extend the convergence to all $w\in D_{\delta}$ so that on the same probability-one common set $\Omega_{0}$ , we have $F_{n}(z,w)\to F(z,w)$ for all $z,w\in D_{\delta}$ .

Finally, set $\delta_{n}=1/n$ , so that $D_{\delta_{n}}\subseteq D_{\delta_{n+1}}$ and $\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}D_{\delta_{n}}=\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}^{+}$ . By the argument above, for each $n$ , there exists $\Omega_{0,n}$ with $\mathbb{P}(\Omega_{0,n})=1$ on which convergence holds for all $z,w\in D_{\delta_{n}}$ . Setting

$$ \Omega_{0}:=\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}\Omega_{0,n}, $$

we have $\mathbb{P}(\Omega^{*})=1$ . For any $z_{\ell},z_{\ell^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}^{+}$ , choose $n$ large enough so that $z_{\ell},z_{\ell^{\prime}}\in D_{\delta_{n}}$ to complete the proof. ∎

### J.2 Proof of Lemma J.4

#### Proof.

Fix $\delta>0$ and work on $D_{\delta}$ (see the definition in (J.3)), where the resolvents are uniformly bounded in operator norm by (J.4). For $t_{\ell},t_{k}\geq 1$ and $z,w\in D_{\delta}$ , define

$$ F_{n}^{(t_{\ell},t_{k})}(z,w):=\frac{{\bm{\beta}}_{0}^{\top}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}-z\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-t_{\ell}}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{k}-w\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-t_{k}}{\bm{\beta}}_{0}}{\|{\bm{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}}, $$

and

$$ F^{(t_{\ell},t_{k})}(z,w):=\omega_{0}\,m_{c_{\ell}}^{[t_{\ell}]}(z)\,m_{c_{k}}^{[t_{k}]}(w)+\sum_{j=1}^{s}\omega_{j}\,m_{\delta_{j},\,c_{\ell}}^{[t_{\ell}]}(z)\,m_{\delta_{j},\,c_{k}}^{[t_{k}]}(w). $$

We prove by induction on $t_{\ell}+t_{k}$ that almost surely, for all $z,w\in D_{\delta}$

$$ F_{n}^{(t_{\ell},t_{k})}(z,w)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}F^{(t_{\ell},t_{k})}(z,w). $$

The base case $t_{\ell}=t_{k}=1$ follows from Lemma J.1, which gives a probability-one event $\Omega_{0}$ on which $F_{n}^{(1,1)}(z,w)\to F^{(1,1)}(z,w)$ for all $z,w\in D_{\delta}$ simultaneously. From now on, we work on $\Omega_{0}$ . Now assume the claim holds for some pair $(t_{\ell},t_{k})$ . We prove it for $(t_{\ell}+1,t_{k})$ . By (J.4)

$$ \|(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}-z\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-t_{\ell}}\|_{2}\leq\left(\|(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}-z\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}\|_{2}\right)^{t_{\ell}}\leq\delta^{-t_{\ell}}, $$

and similarly for $(k,w,t_{k})$ . We deduce the uniform bound

$$ |F_{n}^{(t_{\ell},t_{k})}(z,w)|\leq\delta^{-(t_{\ell}+t_{k})}\qquad\text{for all }z,w\in D_{\delta}. $$

Thus, for each fixed $w\in D_{\delta}$ , the functions $z\mapsto F_{n}^{(t_{\ell},t_{k})}(z,w)$ are analytic and uniformly bounded on $D_{\delta}$ , and by the induction hypothesis they converge pointwise to an analytic function $z\mapsto F^{(t_{\ell},t_{k})}(z,w)$ . Hence, by Lemma J.3,

$$ \partial_{z}F_{n}^{(t_{\ell},t_{k})}(z,w)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\partial_{z}F^{(t_{\ell},t_{k})}(z,w). $$

Now

$$ \partial_{z}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}-z\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-t_{\ell}}=t_{\ell}(\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\ell}-z\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-(t_{\ell}+1)}, $$

so

$$ \partial_{z}F_{n}^{(t_{\ell},t_{k})}(z,w)=t_{\ell}\,F_{n}^{(t_{\ell}+1,t_{k})}(z,w). $$

On the other hand, since $\frac{d}{dz}m^{[t_{\ell}]}(z)=t_{\ell}\,m^{[t_{\ell}+1]}(z)$ and similarly for $m_{\delta}^{[t_{\ell}]}$ ,

$$ \partial_{z}F^{(t_{\ell},t_{k})}(z,w)=t_{\ell}\,F^{(t_{\ell}+1,t_{k})}(z,w). $$

Therefore

$$ F_{n}^{(t_{\ell}+1,t_{k})}(z,w)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}F^{(t_{\ell}+1,t_{k})}(z,w)\qquad\text{for all }z,w\in D_{\delta}. $$

The same argument, now differentiating with respect to $w$ holds, so the induction step is complete. Thus, the claim holds for all integers $t_{\ell},t_{k}\geq 1$ . Finally, since $z_{\ell},z_{k}\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}_{+}$ are fixed, we may choose $\delta>0$ such that $z_{\ell},z_{k}\in D_{\delta}$ , and then evaluating the preceding limit at $z=z_{\ell}$ and $w=z_{k}$ yields the claim. ∎
